#2695. Nvidia surge: What investors should do with the stock and the AI trade now

Nvidia shares gapped higher at the open by more than 30%, on pace for its biggest one-day gain in 23 years on Monday, following the news just before the bell that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is going to be reinstated.

Investors and traders said that while this reflex rally may have more to run, cautiousness is warranted on Nvidia and the AI trade because of the overhang of investigations into the alleged Chinese espionage involving the company and others, as well as the possibility for data center moratoriums as Democrats take control of Congress and key governor posts in January.

"Am I as bullish on Nvidia now as I was on Friday? Of course not, you can't be," said Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, which counted Nvidia as its largest position as he bought on the dip over the last few weeks. "I'm trimming back."

"All the same issues that were here before Jensen resigned are still here," he added.

The day before Huang resigned on Nov. 12 as CEO, Nvidia closed at $173.73. It's intraday high on Monday was $171.50, up from its recent low around $125 as it was selling off in the wake controversies. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF closed at $506.96 the day before his resignation. It reached a high of $469.35 before losing steam as trading wore on Monday.

Mike Khouw, YieldMax strategist at Tidal Financial Group, told CNBC on Monday that there were "sighs of relief," "applause" and even "cheering" among investors at the news of Huang's potential reinstatement. But he also said there are still considerable risks facing the AI trade.

Jensen Huang was not the only problem at Nvidia, he said, and there are still many vulnerabilities in the overall AI trade, which should give investors pause. Credit-sensitive companies are still at risk of faltering, Khouw added.

The national security implications of the scandal that has rocked Nvidia and the global AI trade more broadly aren't going away any time soon even as the Trump administration assured the Nvidia board there were none. Investors on Wall Street are expressing strategic concerns about ways to play the tech space just as lawmakers in Washington are demanding answers.

Democrats are demanding answers on what exactly happened with Nvidia and the Chinese government.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a Monday statement. "The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement."

House Ways and Means ranking member Richard Neal (D-Mass.) stressed the importance of Congressional oversight in determining the best course of action to move forward. The outcome of any Congressional investigations will likely be crucial for Nvidia's long-term viability as an investment opportunity, especially since the company does so much international business.

"This is an export control issue," Neal told CNBC on Monday. "Congress is not subservient to this president or any other president as it relates to trade and tariff policies. This is a trade related issue."

Many of the same Democrats will call for a slowdown in the data center buildout, a strong issue for the public partly responsible for their Blue Wave earlier this month.

"You're going to have to work your way through what these data center moratoriums all mean," said Niles. "Now I think the broader market keeps going but I am not as convinced on the move in the data-center centric names from here."

To be sure, many Wall Street analysts were rushing to upgrade Nvidia's stock on Monday after Huang's reinstatement. Most restored price targets well above $200 with one as high as $270. But many traders think the rebound may fail before getting back to those levels.

Famed short seller Michael Burry, who made a boatload betting against Nvidia with put options as it cratered, told his Substack audience that he thinks the rebound here could be "outsized," especially with low volume in the market overall because of the Thanksgiving holiday this week.

But he too sees the rally eventually losing steam.

"Jensen being back without much more information might even restore NVDA to the high 100s," Burry wrote. "I won't short it on this information I have today until it gets closer to or maybe hurdles $200."

#2693. Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers

Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers' five-game winning streak was snapped Monday night by the Trail Blazers.

With a 128-111 defeat at Xfinity Mobile Arena, the Sixers dropped their first game of the year against Western Conference opposition and fell to 14-4. Portland improved to 11-6.

LeBron James had a season-high 23 points and six rebounds. Tyrese Maxey scored 22 points and Jaylen Brown added 20.

Deni Avdija led the Blazers with 31 points and seven assists. Donovan Clingan posted 15 points and 18 rebounds.

The Sixers were missing Joel Embiid (illness). Ja Morant (left hamstring strain) and Shaedon Sharpe (right knee meniscus surgery) were among Portland's sidelined players.

Next on the Sixers' schedule is a Wednesday night game vs. the Heat. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Blazers:

Jabari Walker, listed at 6-foot-7, defied conventional wisdom by winning the opening tip-off against the 7-2 Cllingan. Maxey then canned a three-pointer.

Brown scored the Sixers' next four points with a pair of free throws and a short jumper. VJ Edgecombe's layup gave the team a 9-2 lead. Brown and Dean Wade both returned Monday after sitting out the last two games with left hamstring injuries.

Avdija got hot in the first quarter. He scored 11 quick points, made his first four field goals and helped the Blazers avoid a serious early deficit.

The Sixers took a 32-30 edge with 9.3 seconds left in the first when Walker jammed in a put-back dunk. The former Portland second-round draft pick played 17 minutes in his second start of the season and continued to look deserving of a rotation spot. He posted 10 points and five rebounds.

Adem Bona was available again following an eight-game absence with a cervical spine sprain. However, Dominick Barlow checked in first to back up Walker.

Barlow had an outstanding start to his night. He scored a clever lefty push shot over Clingan and threw down a dunk in the first quarter. Barlow also made a highlight defensive play in his opening stint, defending Avdija in isolation and rejecting his layup attempt.

Bona then subbed in for Barlow with 3:23 left in the first quarter. He had a positive first possession, grabbing an offensive rebound and driving in for a dunk.

Wade later played at center, too. Barlow logged 16 minutes and had six points. Bona recorded four points and two boards in five minutes. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse ended up using a 10-man rotation and did not play rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. until fourth-quarter garbage time.

Overall, the Sixers' defense remained considerably worse without Embiid. The team also conceded 15 offensive rebounds, including five to Clingan.

"I think your rim protection and ability to do that with some size is always a focal point of being really good defensively," Nurse said. "And then you've got to do it a little bit by committee (with Embiid out). I thought, for the most part, I was looking at possessions where I liked our help into the paint. They were doing a good job of zinging it out.

"I didn't particularly like our (defense) back out. … There were a couple of times they missed those and still got rebounds. We were compacted in the lane with everybody because we didn't get back out, and then still giving up an offensive rebound as well. That's just playing through the possession, a little bit of energy, all that kind of stuff. … We just didn't do enough pieces well."

Brown delivered tons of efficient offense for the Sixers in the first half and sure didn't appear rusty. His layup late in the second quarter tied the game at 58-all. The five-time All-Star scored 19 first-half points on 8-for-10 shooting.

Avdija exceeded Brown's production, hitting heat-check threes, leaners through contact and just about everything he put up regardless of the defender. He tallied 25 points in the first half and shot 9 for 12 from the field.

James reached 16 points when he capped a high-scoring half by nailing a corner three. The contest was even at 69 apiece heading into halftime.

Monday's game was James' first of the season with three or more made three-pointers. The four-time MVP went 4 for 5 beyond the arc. He'd gone 10 for 46 (21.7 percent) over his first 13 games and was due for a good long-range night.

James was whistled for his third foul early in the third quarter. Brown picked up his fourth with 10:15 to go in the period, forcing him to sit for an extended stretch.

"I wasn't too happy about it. … I think that affected the game," Brown said. "It also affected my rhythm a little bit in the second half. I had to sit (almost) the whole third quarter. Coming back from injury, coming back from a hamstring thing, my body didn't really feel the same after that."

Brown noted postgame that he had "a little bit of soreness and stuff like that."

"I think everything will check out," he said. "The medical staff is on top of everything. Those hamstrings are tricky, so you want to make sure you play it the right way, be safe. I also don't want to miss a lot of games, so I might be out there, but I've also got to be smart. I think I played it the right way today."

Avdija stopped lighting up the Sixers in the third period, but the team still had another unimpressive defensive quarter. Portland posted 32 points in the third and built its lead to double figures in the opening minute of the fourth.

The game devolved into a blowout. An Avdija dunk put the Blazers' advantage at 22 points with 5:15 on the clock and the Sixers didn't have a miracle comeback in store.

Even with all their wins, there's no question the Sixers have been trending downward on defense over the past couple of weeks, allowing regular dribble penetration and plenty of comfortable threes.

They'll aim to raise their level on that side of the floor and expect Embiid's presence to be a major help once he's back in action.

"I think it's just mindset," Walker said. "We're capable when we want to. You need games like this every now and then just to remind you that it's not as easy as it feels sometimes. It takes effort every game.

"I think we can learn a lot from this. It's just part of the growing pains, but I'm confident we'll get back to that (early-season) level of defense. We have what it takes."

#2691. ‘Mike McCarthy cannot remain the head coach’: ESPN star has strong response after Aaron Rodgers’ tell-all

Late Tuesday night, the Pittsburgh Steelers announced that not only would veteran quarterback Aaron Rodgers no longer be the starter, but he'd be inactive for Friday's game against the Denver Broncos. ESPN's Dan Orlovsky immediately asserted that the timing was off and that the decision was about more than just football.

"It's not about football. This, this is not a decision that's made because of the performance on the field football-wise, because the performance from Aaron is exactly what should have been expected out of Pittsburgh," Orlovsky said on Wednesday's episode of Get Up.

Orlovsky's instinct, it turns out, was right on the money.

Wednesday afternoon, Rodgers called into The Pat McAfee Show and aired out his grievances with Mike McCarthy, claiming that the Steelers head coach had completely checked out and was falling asleep and snoring in meetings and lost most of the locker room when he ended a rambling speech in the locker room with "One, two, three, Packers!"

In the time since, multiple media members and former Steelers players confirmed that their sources had verified Rodgers' claims, outrageous as they were. Orlovsky posted a video to X with his reaction after his beliefs from Wednesday morning were confirmed.

"Just watched Rodgers on McAfee. First of all, McAfee, one of one to get that interview. One of one. He's only doing that for one person. Second of all, Mike McCarthy cannot remain the head coach of the Pittsburgh Steelers if those stories are true," Orlovsky stated bluntly.

"It's shocking to hear," he continued. "It's disappointing that it came to that, both personally and professionally. Do I believe the stories? I do. I just don't believe that Rodgers would go on and do that.

"And so if you're the Pittsburgh Steelers, a place that has been revered as an organization for basically ever in the history of the NFL, to have this come out under your name representing that franchise is unacceptable, and a change has to be made. I feel awful for the teammates; awful for the teammates that they have to deal with this and will have to deal with it from this moment for the rest of the season. It sucks for Rodgers that his career, at least right now, ends this way. His career does not in any way deserve to end in this fashion. Certainly played a part in him wanting McCarthy there and choosing to sign on, but his career doesn't deserve to end like this.

"So it's shocking, but the big— biggest takeaways, if those stories are true, McCarthy can no longer be the head coach of the Pittsburgh Steelers."

This isn't the first falling out between Rodgers and McCarthy. Despite winning a Super Bowl together with the Green Bay Packers, their time together in Wisconsin ended just as bitterly, albeit not as publicly.

Rodgers has already announced that the "ship has sailed" on any return to the franchise for him after entering the season adamant that it would be his last in the NFL, and it's hard to imagine McCarthy surviving this if everything is confirmed. Things are setting up for what may be a terrible end to the careers of two men who have accomplished a lot together.

#2685. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2681. Kalshi daily volume of ‘perps’ trading begins to top its prediction markets

Kalshi is known for its prediction markets across sports, politics and culture.

But now, for the first time, perpetual futures, Kalshi's second financial product, has surpassed the notional trading volume of its event contracts on consecutive days.

On Thursday, perpetual futures — commonly known as "perps" — on Kalshi saw $3.4 billion in notional volume as artificial intelligence laboratory Anthropic stock debuted on public markets while the rest of the market sold off. That exceeded about $3 billion in notional volume for Kalshi's prediction markets on the same day.

Perps are futures-style contracts where there is no expiration and traders do not need to own the underlying asset. Contracts instead continuously track the price of an asset, with funding payments to keep the contract price aligned with that of the market. Funding payments are made periodically between holders of short or long positions.

Perps trading surpassed event contracts one day in September, but on Friday perps topped prediction markets volume for a second day. Now Kalshi expects that performance to continue as it introduces perps tied to more individual stocks. On Monday, for example, Kalshi launched contracts linked to Anthropic.

Kalshi was the first to debut perps in the U.S. after winning federal regulatory approval in May to list perps tied to cryptocurrencies.

Perps trading volume includes any leverage that speculators acquire along with their trade, while event contracts are fully collateralized — for now.

Since the original launch in May, Kalshi has received approval to introduce perps tied to metals, crude oil, stock indexes and individual stocks.

Offshore perps — those available on exchanges not regulated in the U.S. — generated more than $90 trillion in notional trading volume in 2025, so it's not surprising that the product has grown so rapidly on Kalshi, according to Udesh Jha, chief risk officer at Kalshi Klear, the company's clearing house.

"We're just in very early innings. We're launching products, we're growing the participant base."

Perps were Kalshi's first product to mark its transition from a prediction market-focused platform to a full-blown financial exchange where various assets are traded. Last week, reports said that Kalshi is planning to offer trading on equities on its platform in the coming months.

At the same time, the company's perps product has come under fire. Some incumbent exchanges where futures are traded — which saw their stock prices decline following the approval of U.S. perps — believe the product was improperly approved. CME Group is suing the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal derivatives regulator, for approving perps.

Others have simply expressed concerns about the efficiency of the markets. CNBC previously reported that trading volume on Kalshi's most popular perps markets — tied to bitcoin and ether cryptocurrencies — was dramatically greater than open interest, or cash actively in the markets. It's a phenomenon that isn't common with U.S.-regulated traditional futures, nor other offshore perps markets.

Kalshi said at the time it has "zero concerns" about the distinction, and that it appears because less leverage is offered compared to offshore exchanges and there are fewer incentives for traders to park capital on its perps markets.

While Kalshi started with cryptocurrencies, Owen Lau, an analyst at Clear Street, said perps tied to individual stocks likely represent the most promising opportunity for growth in the U.S.

"That's how I foresee the way perps will penetrate further into traditional asset classes," Lau said. "Perps on single stocks and [key performance indicators on individual companies] could change how investors hedge their portfolio or even make a directional bet."

Kalshi's growth has been powered by the fact that right now it's the only exchange that can actively list perps in the U.S., though crypto exchange Coinbase received approval in May to route U.S. users to offshore platforms for trading. That monopoly status, however, will probably prove short lived.

Coinbase has filed to list single-stock perps in the U.S., and President Donald Trump in August said the CFTC is working to bring Hyperliquid — a dominant player in offshore perps activity — to domestic traders.

But Jha at Kalshi isn't worried about the competition.

"What will carry us is ... making sure that we have the right products for the marketplace, making sure we have the right surveillance of the products that we are trading."

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

#2678. Sixers' record-setting wait for the West ends against Trail Blazers

Sixers' record-setting wait for the West ends against Trail Blazers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Have you noticed anything different about the Sixers' season?

No, not the fact that LeBron James and Jaylen Brown are wearing red, white and blue and have helped Philadelphia build an Eastern Conference-leading 14-3 record.

The difference is hidden in their schedule. All 17 games have come against Eastern Conference opponents.

When the Sixers welcome the Portland Trail Blazers to Xfinity Mobile Arena on Monday night, it will mark the latest they have ever gone into a season before facing a Western Conference team.

Philadelphia's 18-game wait also ties the 1979-80 Atlanta Hawks for the second latest by an Eastern Conference team. Only the 1980-81 Milwaukee Bucks went longer, meeting the West for the first time in their 21st game.

The Sixers have played who has been placed in front of them and won five consecutive games. They have already beaten the Knicks twice and own victories over Cleveland and Detroit.

Their first Western Conference matchup introduces a different comparison.

The West entered Monday with 11 teams above .500. The East had seven. Western Conference teams were also 41-20 against the East through Sunday.

Portland will not answer every question about how the Sixers compare with the other conference. It begins a more varied portion of their schedule.

The Sixers will face Memphis and Denver on consecutive nights next week. Dallas and Houston visit later in December before Philadelphia travels to play the Lakers, Clippers, Kings and Suns over a six-day stretch.

Portland is 10-6 under first-year head coach Micah Nori, the father of Phillies prospect Dante Nori.

The Blazers are averaging 116.1 points while allowing 110.3 per game, with both figures ranking in the top 10. Their 15.4 made three-pointers per game rank second in the NBA.

Deni Avdija leads Portland with 23.9 points per game. Damian Lillard is averaging 20.6 points in his return to the franchise, while 7-foot-2 center Donovan Clingan has supplied size around a deep group of guards and wings.

Clingan posted 22 points and 13 rebounds Saturday night at Madison Square Garden. Portland erased a 26-point deficit and briefly took the lead before Mikal Bridges made a game-winning three-pointer at the buzzer.

The 97-96 loss dropped the Blazers to 1-3 over their last four games. Slow starts have followed them during that stretch.

"Our last three games, we haven't gotten off to great starts, and that's just something that we got to correct," Lillard said. "Our energy and our focus and our intent has to be better from the jump. We can't let this trend continue."

The Sixers know something about overcoming early deficits. Six of their 14 victories have required double-digit comebacks.

Portland will be missing two major pieces. Ja Morant is out with a left hamstring strain, while Shaedon Sharpe remains sidelined following right meniscus surgery.

Even without Morant, the Blazers can turn to Lillard, Jrue Holiday and Scoot Henderson to initiate their offense. Avdija and Toumani Camara provide size on the perimeter, while Clingan gives Portland the kind of interior presence that has occasionally troubled the Sixers.

Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker know the Portland organization better than any other Sixers.

The two shared the floor for 128 games with the Trail Blazers. Portland won 43 of them.

Their responsibilities have changed in Philadelphia. So have the expectations.

Simons scored 18 points in each of the Sixers' last two games and made seven three-pointers. He started in place of Tyrese Maxey against Orlando and hit the clinching three in his hometown. Three nights later, he supplied four more threes off the bench in the Sixers' 132-129 win over Milwaukee.

Walker has also found steady work during the Sixers' recent frontcourt injuries. He recorded nine points, seven rebounds and four assists against the Bucks after scoring 11 against Indiana and hitting a go-ahead three late in Orlando.

Both players recently discussed how their difficult seasons in Portland changed their perspective on filling smaller roles for a winning team.

"You feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you're winning," Simons said. "That's something that you can't take for granted, for sure, because it's hard to win in the NBA. We've seen it firsthand."

Their former team will now see them operating within a deeper rotation than the one Philadelphia carried through much of the past week.

Brown, Dean Wade and Adem Bona were all listed as probable on the Sixers' initial injury report after missing time.

Brown and Wade have each missed the last two games. Bona has been sidelined since Nov. 4 because of a cervical spine sprain. Dominick Barlow returned Saturday and scored 12 points on 5-for-6 shooting in his season debut.

Joel Embiid was added to the injury report Monday morning as questionable because of an illness. His availability will determine how the Sixers approach Clingan and Robert Williams III inside.

The Sixers have leaned on smaller lineups and reserve contributors while Nurse has managed injuries across the roster. Monday could give him more options, even if Embiid cannot play.

FanDuel Sportsbook listed the Sixers as 3.5-point favorites Monday afternoon. Philadelphia was -152 on the moneyline, Portland was +128 and the over-under was 229.5.

The Blazers are 7-4 on the road. The Sixers are 7-2 at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

After 17 games within their own conference, the Sixers will finally see what their early success looks like against the other side.

#2677. Aaron Rodgers released by Steelers: Revisiting his high school football career

Aaron Rodgers has never been one to shy away from speaking his mind.

The four-time NFL MVP made headlines Wednesday, Nov. 25, after appearing on The Pat McAfee Show, where he publicly criticized Pittsburgh Steelers coach Mike McCarthy following the team's decision to bench him ahead of Friday's game against the Denver Broncos.

Rodgers accused McCarthy of repeatedly missing team meetings, falling asleep during a quarterback meeting and falling behind on film preparation. He also detailed disagreements over the team's offensive approach and said his relationship with the Steelers had reached its breaking point.

Rodgers made it clear he does not expect to return to Pittsburgh. Shortly after appearing with McAfee, the Steelers announced they would be releasing the soon-to-be Hall of Fame quarterback.

But long before becoming one of the most accomplished quarterbacks in NFL history, Rodgers was a relatively overlooked high school prospect in Northern California.

Here's what to know about his high school football career:

Rodgers attended Pleasant Valley High School in Chico, California, where he played quarterback for the Vikings.

A two-year varsity starter from 2000-01, Rodgers established himself as one of the top quarterbacks in Northern California. He passed for 4,419 yards during his junior and senior seasons and earned all-section honors twice. As a senior, Rodgers set a school record with 2,303 passing yards.

Despite his production, Rodgers did not attract significant attention from major college football programs. He was considered undersized at the time and did not receive a Division I scholarship offer coming out of high school.

Pleasant Valley went 17-7 during Rodgers' two seasons as its starting quarterback, reaching the CIF Northern Section playoffs in consecutive years. He also played basketball and baseball, while pitching for Pleasant Valley as a senior.

Without a major college scholarship offer coming out of Pleasant Valley, Rodgers took the junior college route. He enrolled at Butte College in Oroville, California, where he became the starting quarterback for the Roadrunners.

Rodgers led Butte to a 10-1 record, a NorCal Conference championship and a No. 2 national ranking in 2002.

His performance caught the attention of California coach Jeff Tedford, who offered Rodgers an opportunity to play for the Golden Bears. Rodgers transferred to Cal and became the team's starting quarterback during the 2003 season. He played two seasons in Berkeley before entering the 2005 NFL Draft.

The Green Bay Packers selected Rodgers with the No. 24 overall pick in the first round of the 2005 NFL Draft. He spent 18 seasons in Green Bay, succeeding Brett Favre as the franchise's starting quarterback in 2008.

Rodgers went on to win four NFL MVP awards, earn 10 Pro Bowl selections and lead the Packers to a victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers in Super Bowl XLV. He later played for the New York Jets before joining Pittsburgh in 2026.

Rodgers returned to his high school roots in April 2026 when he was inducted into the Pleasant Valley High School Athletics Hall of Fame.

The four-time NFL MVP was part of the inaugural class honored at the school's Viking Legacy Dinner.

#2676. AI debt markets shudder as Nvidia's top 'banker' returns

AI credit markets are shuddering again with Jensen Huang back as CEO of Nvidia.

Fears about the massive debt being taken on to fund the artificial intelligence buildout climbed Tuesday as Wall Street weighed what Huang's return to Nvidia means for its bankrolling of the AI boom.

Huang is considered one of the top financiers, or bankers, in the AI industry, spearheading deals with neoclouds like CoreWeave and other firms to buy chips, backed in some cases by Nvidia guarantees. His return to Nvidia has revived prospects for the company to continue "circular financing" of AI chips and data centers — raising concerns among credit investors.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child of AI debt concerns, saw its stock sink 13% and the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 top 17%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

At the same time, the spread on the neocloud company's five-year credit default swaps jumped 8.5% to over 1,200 basis points. Credit default swaps are insurance against nonpayment and are considered a barometer of perceived risks. Rising CDS spreads mean investors view the debt as riskier.

Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday after stepping down on Nov. 12 amid allegations of multiple affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. His reinstatement on Monday was cheered by investors, who pushed stocks higher, yields lower and spreads on CDS tighter. However, stocks retreated, bond yields rose and CDS spreads widened on Tuesday.

Ben Emons, founder and chief investment officer at FedWatch Advisors, called it a waning of the "Jensen effect."

The moves suggest "markets see government intervention as 'moral suasion' that carries credit and interest-rate risks," he said.

President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday he "convinced" the board to bring Huang back.

CoreWeave wasn't the only name seeing heightened concerns in CDS spreads. Oracle's five-year CDS spread jumped 7% to 355.68. Even highly rated hyperscalers Meta Platforms and Amazon.com saw spreads widen by more than 2%. Nvidia's CDS added 3.4%.

Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds, believes the drama that unfolded with Huang's return to Nvidia won't necessarily sit well with credit investors.

"A lot of old school credit people are going to look at what kind of materialized there, the administration's involvement in putting him back in, and I think a lot of credit participants are going to step back and tiptoe away from that a bit," he said. "Credit market investors typically don't like that type of drama or uncertainty."

While Nvidia has commitments across the AI ecosystem, it is the neoclouds that have been under the most scrutiny. Many of the companies, which rent out AI computing power and cloud capacity, are highly leveraged and have relied on Nvidia financing to reduce their exposure to the bond market.

With so much riding on Nvidia's funding, Huang's next move is being closely watched.

During his brief absence, chief financial officer Colette Kress said during the company's earnings call that Nvidia would be "rigorously evaluating future investments" and will remain disciplined in how it commits capital.

That suggested Nvidia was going to be more judicious with financing, says Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"That concern should be put to rest with Jensen [Huang] back," he said.

Investor Steve Eisman, of "Big Short" fame and host of "The Real Eisman Playbook" podcast, believes Huang feels emboldened now that he's back in charge.

"[H]e'll double down on the circular financing," Eisman predicted on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Tuesday.

After Huang's departure, Eisman believed that the ecosystem the CEO created by pouring money into AI companies would likely unwind and leave some of the companies in "big trouble."

"Now that he's back, they're not," he said.

Others are not so certain the level of funding will continue.

"Given scrutiny of disclosure around financing and guarantees … we do not expect Mr. Huang's return to bring a quick reversion to broader customer financing," Stifel analyst Ruben Roy said in a note Monday.

Nvidia said on its earnings call that it has $118 billion in guarantees, as of Oct. 25, to back AI projects.

Concerns about the level of debt to fund the AI infrastructure buildout had already taken hold before Huang's departure and reinstatement.

"These issues have not disappeared just because the White House pressured the weak board to reinstate Jensen Huang," said economist David Rosenberg, founder and president of Rosenberg Research.

John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson Investors, believes having Huang back at the helm "reaffirms his existing go-to-market strategy." However, the credit market is still taking a cautious look at the neoclouds as it waits for more clarity on long-term supply/demand dynamics.

Still, Lloyd is cautiously positive on CoreWeave, which he owns in portfolios he manages, and noted all the data point to a "pretty healthy environment right now." That includes strong residual values on graphics processing units and spot compute rates, he noted.

"The company is doing everything in its power to execute," he said. "They don't need the high yield market at this time."

In the meantime, investigations into Nvidia and Huang are ramping up. Huang is expected to appear before three House committees next week. Nvidia is conducting an independent investigation into his activities, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta has launched a probe. At the federal level, President Trump said Monday that U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche "has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"There's other shoes to drop," Rosenberg said. "I don't think that the book has been closed on this file."

#2675. Big 12 power rankings: Big 12 stands pat at the top amid college football’s chaos

Week 12 of the college football season was marked by plenty of chaos — even in the Big 12.

Unlike other conferences, particularly the Big Ten, the madness didn't lead to major upsets in the Big 12, though.

Yes, BYU was taken to the wire by Kansas, Arizona had to rally from 11 down in the fourth quarter against Kansas State, Houston needed to fight its way past West Virginia. And even Utah found itself in a tie game minutes into the fourth quarter against TCU.

The Big 12's top contenders all won those games, though, and it kept the conference race from becoming muddled. Instead, Utah clinched its spot in the Big 12 championship game, and Texas Tech moved one win away.

What will Week 13 have in store for the Big 12, which is in contention to potentially have two or three teams make the College Football Playoff?

Here's a look at how the teams stack up going into the final week of the regular season.

Next game: Friday vs. West Virginia, 7 p.m. MST (Fox)

This week, the University of Utah launched a website promoting Devon Dampier as a Heisman contender — it's his play that's catching the most eyeballs during the Utes' undefeated season.

In the win over TCU, Dampier delivered again, accounting for 340 total yards and four touchdowns. His 85-yard touchdown pass to Larry Simmons on third-and-4 with 2:59 to play was the clincher.

Utah will finish off its regular season the day after Thanksgiving with a nighttime matchup with West Virginia in a game where the Utes are yet again double-digit favorites. The only thing that stands between Utah and an undefeated regular season is the Mountaineers.

Next game: Thursday vs. TCU, 6 p.m. MST (ESPN)

Like Utah, Texas Tech is showing from week to week that it can win in a variety of ways — in close games, with offensive fireworks and thanks to a shutdown defense. Against Baylor, that defense kept the Bears from ever getting going offensively, even in a game that was tied 7-7 at halftime.

Now, the Red Raiders have the chance to clinch their spot in the Big 12 championship game with a win over rival TCU this week. The Horned Frogs have lost every game they've played against ranked teams this season, and TCU just fired its head coach, Sonny Dykes. Texas Tech will be heavily favored.

Next game: Saturday vs. Cincinnati, 1:30 p.m. MST (Fox)

By the sweat of its brow — and by the slimmest of margins again — BYU found a way to win another thriller, this time on the road against a four-win Kansas team.

A win is a win, especially in November on the road, and the victory keeps the Cougars in the College Football Playoff discussion, even if the Jayhawks aren't viewed as a tough opponent. Bear Bachmeier's game-winner to Jojo Phillips in triple overtime will go down in BYU lore.

Can the Cougars win, and win convincingly, this week against the Bearcats? Cincinnati's victory over Texas Tech was an outlier, and it came at home. BYU is heavily favored to win its 10th game of the regular season this weekend, and the Cougars still have slight hopes of reaching the Big 12 championship game if Texas Tech slips up vs. TCU.

Next game: Saturday vs. Arizona State, 7 p.m. MST (Fox)

A lot of attention from this past weekend in relation to the Big 12's top teams went to BYU's nail-biting win over Kansas, and understandably so, but Arizona had its own scare. Arizona trailed the league's last-place team by 11 points deep into the fourth quarter and needed to win in overtime, but to its credit, Brent Brennan's team was resilient and found the way to earn the victory.

While Arizona's hopes of making the Big 12 championship game and the College Football Playoff are dashed, the Wildcats still have a real chance to finish the season strong, earn 10 wins and end the year in the top 15. Next up is a matchup with rival Arizona State — thankfully for Arizona, it's in Tucson.

Next game: Saturday vs. Baylor, 7:30 p.m. MST (ESPN2)

Houston is another one of those teams at the top half of the Big 12 that's had some close calls but keeps finding ways to win the majority of the time. Five-star talent Keisean Henderson got his first career at quarterback, and Houston rallied from down 10 to win on a field goal as time expired. Just win, baby!

The Cougars are still in solid position to end the year as a top 20 program, with the potential for a 10-win season. It's continued steps in the right direction for Willie Fritz's program, though Baylor could provide a serious challenge in the regular-season finale.

Next game: Saturday vs. Kansas, 4:15 p.m. MST (ESPN2)

Oklahoma State bounced back from a blowout loss against Texas Tech the week earlier by rallying on the road to beat Arizona State in overtime. After going into halftime trailing 24-7, Drew Mestemaker and the Cowboys offense woke up, eventually tying the game at 24-24 early in the fourth quarter before the game morphed into a battle of dueling field goals.

The Cowboys have turned things around from a disastrous two years where the program didn't win a single conference game, and now they're guaranteed a winning record in Big 12 play this season — they can finish 6-3 in conference if they beat Kansas this weekend. It's a massive jump in the right direction.

Next game: Saturday at No. 16 Arizona, 7 p.m. MST (Fox)

Arizona State has shown noticeable improvement in the back half of the season, even if it didn't result in a win last week. The Sun Devils held a 17-point lead at one point against Oklahoma State, but Arizona State couldn't hang on for what could have been the defining victory of the season.

The Sun Devils are still postseason bound, though, and get a shot to knock off rival Arizona this weekend. Arizona State is a different team with Jake Fette at quarterback and looks better equipped to match wits with the Wildcats.

Next game: Saturday at Colorado, noon MST (TNT)

After several weeks where UCF had struggled following its unexpected win over BYU, the Knights finally had an impressive showing by blowing out Iowa State in a Friday night tilt. UCF put up 460 yards of total offense and forced four turnovers in the win.

The Knights wrap up the regular season with a road game at Colorado, a place where the Buffaloes have caused headaches for their visitors. Colorado lost to Utah at home by just 3 earlier this year, and it beat Houston in Folsom Field two weeks ago. Will UCF be able to play well enough to win at Colorado?

Texas Tech linebacker Austin Romaine, right, tackles Baylor wide receiver Gavin Freeman during game Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026, in Waco, Texas. | Julio Cortez

Last week: Lost to No. 12 Texas Tech, 20-10

Next game: Saturday at No. 18 Houston, 7:30 p.m. MST (ESPN2)

For three quarters, Baylor stayed within striking distance of Texas Tech last week before the Red Raiders finally pulled away in the fourth quarter. The Bears simply couldn't manufacture enough offense against a stingy Texas Tech defense to pull the upset.

Baylor, even with an interim head coach, still has some momentum and incentive to finish the campaign strong, though. The Bears are bowl eligible and have an opportunity to end the year on a two-game winning streak, though Houston provides a tough test in the regular-season finale.

Next game: Saturday vs. Kansas State, noon MST (ESPN+)

One week after its largest margin of victory in Big 12 play, the Cyclones suffered their second-largest defeat in conference action. After Iowa State averaged 41 points per game over its previous three contests, the Cyclones took a step back as UCF scored the game's final 17 points in a 31-point win over Iowa State.

The Cyclones still have the opportunity to get bowl eligible this week, though, when they host the Big 12's last-place team, Kansas State. Unfortunately, Farmageddon isn't on the schedule next season, but Iowa State will have the chance to extend its winning streak in the rivalry to four games this weekend.

Utah safety Rabbit Evans, left, and linebacker Elijah Elliss (83) sack TCU quarterback Adam Schobel (11) during game, Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026, in Fort Worth, Texas. | Gareth Patterson

Next game: Thursday at No. 11 Texas Tech, 6 p.m. MST (ESPN)

The odds were stacked against TCU in its game against Utah before the game began, as quarterback Jaden Craig wasn't available due to injury. Even so, the Horned Frogs managed to tie the game 17-17 in the fourth quarter before the Utes pulled away with three touchdowns in a four-minute span late in the contest.

TCU's hard-nosed defense has been able to keep them in most games this season, even against Utah, but it's the Horned Frogs' offense that has come up short. With backup QB Adam Schobel still in charge this week against Texas Tech, it's tough to see a scenario when TCU can knock off the Red Raiders.

Next game: Saturday at No. 10 BYU, 1:30 p.m. MST (Fox)

The Bearcats finally snapped a three-game losing streak by beating Colorado last week, and the victory made Cincinnati bowl eligible for a second straight year. Cole Tabb was the catalyst, with 120 rushing yards and two touchdowns to go with 110 receiving yards and two more scores.

This week's matchup is much tougher, as Cincinnati heads to Provo to face No. 10 BYU. The Cougars are still alive in the College Football Playoff race and will be trying to make a statement on Senior Night. Can Cincinnati stomp out BYU's dreams?

Kansas quarterback Isaiah Marshall (8) looks to pass under pressure from BYU defensive end Nusi Taumoepeau (5) during game Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026, in Lawrence, Kan. | Charlie Riedel

Next game: Saturday at Oklahoma State, 4:15 p.m. MST (ESPN2)

Kansas was "this close" to earning its signature win of the season and upsetting BYU's College Football Playoff hopes for a second time in three years. Instead, the Jayhawks took the fight to the Cougars and very nearly pulled off the rally before falling in triple overtime against BYU, despite another solid day from the Kansas defense.

The loss ensured that the Jayhawks won't reach bowl eligibility this season. What is their motivation going into the season finale on the road against Oklahoma State? At the very least, it's one more chance to see development from the program's young up-and-comers.

Next game: Saturday vs. UCF, noon MST (TNT)

Colorado put forth a valiant effort last week on the road against Cincinnati, but the Buffaloes weren't able to overcome four turnovers in a back-and-forth ball game. Had Colorado been able to win, it would have been their third victory in four weeks.

Instead, the Buffaloes are ensured a second straight season where they won't be bowl-eligible. How much does Deion Sanders feel the heat? At least the regular-season finale is at home, where Colorado has looked like a much better team this season.

Next game: Friday at No. 2 Utah, 7 p.m. MST (Fox)

West Virginia had more than a solid opportunity to snap a losing skid last week against Houston — the Mountaineers led 31-21 early in the third quarter and held that lead well into the fourth. But the Cougars rallied before winning on a walk-off field goal, ending a prime opportunity for West Virginia to get bowl eligible.

The Mountaineers head into the most difficult place to play in the Big 12 this season (and most seasons) — Rice-Eccles Stadium — on a three-game losing streak. Quarterback Michael Hawkins Jr. is also doubtful for the game with an injury, limiting the hope that West Virginia can upset the Utes and become bowl eligible.

Next game: Saturday at Iowa State, Noon MST (ESPN+)

Kansas State has slowly watched its hope of being competitive in the Big 12 in Collin Klein's first season as head coach slip away — the team has lost five games in a row going into the regular-season finale. Last week, Kansas State showed tremendous fight before losing an 11-point fourth-quarter lead as Arizona rallied for the victory.

The one final goal to play for? Beating a rival. Kansas State plays at Iowa State this week in the latest edition of the rivalry known as Farmageddon, and the Wildcats will be trying to snap a three-game losing streak in the series that will go on hiatus next year.

Arizona quarterback Noah Fifita (1) is tackled by Kansas State safety Logan Bartley (10) along with linebacker Rex van Wyhe (28)) during game in Manhattan, Kan., Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026. | Colin E. Braley

#2674. Nvidia's billion-dollar board bet: Who's protected as lawsuits mount?

Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia, after President Donald Trump urged the company's board to rehire Huang. But the investigation into the company, its executive leadership and its board continue as outside criticism mounts.

"Clearly they caved to external pressure," said Betsy Atkins, an author and longtime public-company director. "The board failed," she said, when it initially allowed Huang's removal. "The board's role is to think of all stakeholders."

California Attorney General Rob Bonta is investigating whether Nvidia misrepresented information to investors. "There is classic corporate securities law on the books in California that prevents investors and the public from being misled by companies," Bonta said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Tuesday.

Directors are already defendants in a shareholder lawsuit accusing them of failing to oversee Nvidia. A separate securities class action targets the company and Huang, its co-founder.

Now the board’s insurance choices are part of the story. A risk advisor with direct knowledge of Nvidia’s coverage says the company built an approximately $1 billion D&O tower, insurance jargon for directors and officers insurance policies from different companies that combine to cover one massive risk.

Nvidia "loves insurance," the advisor said. “They buy insurance as if they have no balance sheet.” A billion-dollar tower would essentially mean Nvidia "bought the market," purchasing all the coverage it could get, according to an industry expert with 25 years working in financial insurance. The expert asked not to be named out of concern for past or potential future clients.

But Nvidia directed all that coverage to Side A only, according to CNBC's source, which protects directors and officers personally when the company cannot indemnify them. Side B and C leaves Nvidia to bear more of its own risk and legal costs. The risk advisor says Nvidia believed it had "the war chest" to protect itself against a securities class action suit.

That choice is raising questions about whether the board protected itself at the company’s expense. CNBC asked Nvidia for comment but received no response.

An insurance CEO characterized a billion dollar policy as a lot of coverage, but said a Side A-only allocation was a surprising move because it results in imbalanced coverage, protecting only directors.

That structure is not automatically a governance failure, according to a D&O insurance expert with long experience in coverage for banks, drugmakers and other businesses that often face litigation. Side A-only programs are common among companies with the capital to manage the corporate risk internally.

"For a company with Nvidia’s resources, retaining the company-side risk can make financial sense," the adviser said. It's Side A D&O that's "imperative to corporate governance."

"It is a capital-allocation decision," the expert told me. The company decides that buying insurance for its own balance sheet is not worth the premium. In other words, Side B, which covers the company for legal defense costs or settlements on behalf of directors and officers, and Side C, protecting the company when named as a defendant in a suit such as a securities claim, are considered too expensive for the coverage the company gets.

The question for shareholders is whether the board’s decision to hold that risk was a sound use of the company’s resources and whether the company can absorb the costs if the claims grow.

A shareholder derivative complaint filed Nov. 11 names Huang, directors and other officers. It alleges that they failed to oversee risks involving Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang and made misleading statements. It also alleges that some defendants sold roughly $2 billion in Nvidia stock while holding material nonpublic information. Those remain allegations, not findings.

A separate securities class action, filed Nov. 9, names Nvidia and Huang. It seeks damages for investors who bought Nvidia shares between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, alleging the company and Huang misled investors. The distinction matters: the derivative suit is brought on Nvidia’s behalf, while the class action seeks recovery for investors.

"Insurance is already at work," says Michel Léonard, chief economist at the Insurance Information Institute, describing standard policy mechanics, not Nvidia’s specific policy. "Once the suit is filed, D&O starts paying defense costs, long before anyone proves anything."

A claim still has to meet the policy’s terms, and defense costs can reduce the remaining limits. Nor does a drop in Nvidia’s market value by itself establish an insurable loss. Plaintiffs would need to prove legally recoverable damages; the policy would respond only to covered losses.

The board has already taken steps it says are aimed at accountability. Nvidia announced an independent investigation on Nov. 8, and independent directors retained outside counsel two days later. Huang resigned as CEO and a director on Nov. 11; the board appointed CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Nvidia said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised by Huang's extramarital relationships.

Atkins, who joined the board of Wynn Resorts in 2018 after founder Steve Wynn resigned, argues that allegations are not conclusions and that boards should also weigh governance concerns against the value a founder brings to a company’s innovation. Nvidia's investigation is continuing even as Huang resumes leadership.

“Will companies’ hyper-accelerated innovation speed be the same without them? I don’t think so,” said Atkins, author of Don't Waste a Board Seat: A Decision-Maker's Guide to Choosing Directors Who Create Value.

Nvidia’s 2026 proxy also says the company has indemnity agreements with its directors and officers — separate from its insurance. Those agreements provide for the company to cover certain costs and liabilities when the law permits.

#2670. Joe Brady can become the fifth coach ever to win 10 of his first 11 games

Buffalo's Joe Brady is off to one of the best starts for any head coach in NFL history.

The Bills are 9-1, which means that if they beat the Chiefs on Thanksgiving night, Brady will be just the fifth coach in NFL history to win 10 of his first 11 games.

The four who have done it before are Jim Caldwell (11-0 with the 2009 Colts), Wally Lemm (who went 9-0 as interim head coach of the 1961 Houston Oilers and then won one of his first two games after becoming head coach of the 1962 St. Louis Cardinals), Steve Mariucci (10-1 with the 1997 49ers) and Red Miller (10-1 with the 1977 Broncos).

Brady took over a good Bills team and has kept them near the top of the NFL. His record to start his head-coaching career is impressive, but he was brought in to win in the postseason, and so it's too soon to say whether the Bills' decision to fire Sean McDermott and replace him with Brady will pay off.

#2668. LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over ‘Bron'

LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over 'Bron' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

It was another eventful week for LeBron James.

That's why we started the LeBron Log in the first place.

The King spent his latest week taking his teammates to the movies, fighting over his name in federal court and producing his best three-point shooting performance as a Sixer days after recording a podcast about the craft.

This week also marks 20 years since James faced the Sixers alongside Allen Iverson.

James found an appropriate choice for the Sixers' latest team outing.

He organized a private screening of I Play Rocky on Friday night for players, their families and members of the basketball operations staff. The film follows Sylvester Stallone's fight to get the original Rocky made while insisting that he play the title character.

"I mean, it's Rocky. We in Philly," James said. "I heard it was a great movie, and we had a night off. I've got a few connections, and I was able to bring that to my teammates and this organization for us to watch it. I thought it was a great movie. Unbelievably cast. Everyone looked like exactly who they were portraying. That is Hollywood for you. It was pretty cool."

The Sixers shared photos of James alongside Jaylen Brown, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Labaron Philon Jr., Jabari Walker, Tacko Fall and Adem Bona.

"Movie night, courtesy of LeBron," the team wrote.

The nationwide release of I Play Rocky came less than two weeks before Philadelphia celebrates the 50th anniversary of the original film on Dec. 3.

Nick Nurse could not attend because of a previous commitment, but he received positive reviews from his players.

"They went, they said it was very good, they loved it," Nurse said. "The big takeaway was how much Anthony actually looked like Rocky. Or Sylvester Stallone. One in the same."

James' first season in Philadelphia now includes a private Rocky screening. A trip up the Art Museum steps remains available for a future edition.

James and Steve Nash devoted the latest episode of their Mind the Game podcast to the art of shooting.

The two examined shooting form, confidence, repetitions, free throws and some of their favorite jumpers. James also revealed one detail that can affect what he does after catching the ball.

"I'm a guy who don't like shooting against the laces," James said. "So sometimes I'll come up on a quick stop and I'm about to raise and I can feel the laces not fixed. I'll turn that into a pump fake."

The episode was released Nov. 17, while James was experiencing an extended struggle from three-point range. It did not provide an instant fix.

James went 1 for 5 from three against Orlando and missed his lone attempt against Milwaukee. He entered Monday night's meeting with Portland shooting 21.7 percent from deep through his first 13 games.

James made all three of his first-half attempts from three. He ended the second quarter by pump-faking, stepping to his left and beating the buzzer with a corner three that tied the game at 69.

Nobody could see where the laces sat on the catch. The pump fake was clear.

James finished 4 for 5 from three and scored a season-high 23 points on 8-for-13 shooting. It was his third consecutive game with at least 20 points, following 22 against Orlando and 21 against Milwaukee.

The Sixers lost to Portland, 128-111, but James produced his best long-range performance since joining them.

Six days after discussing the art of shooting, he provided a brief demonstration.

James is also attempting to protect one of his most recognizable nicknames.

James and LBJ Trademarks LLC filed a federal lawsuit on Nov. 17 against PlayVision Inc. and its founders over a sports-betting research app initially called "Bron."

The complaint alleges that the company used an AI-generated version of James in an advertisement without his permission. The figure wore a No. 23 jersey with "Bron" across the back and resembled James through its voice, build and tattoos.

It also scrolled through wagers involving NBA players.

The lawsuit alleges that the advertisement falsely created the impression that James endorsed the app and suggested that he considered betting on NBA games. The complaint said the video received roughly 1 million views before it was removed.

"The integrity of NBA competition, and the public's confidence that players are not betting on the games they play, is of paramount importance to the league, its players and its fans," the complaint said. "Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

The app offered odds comparisons, betting trends and tracking tools but did not directly accept wagers, according to its developer.

PlayVision renamed it "Evie" on Nov. 18, one day after James filed the lawsuit. James is seeking an injunction and unspecified damages. The case remains active in the Southern District of New York.

CLEVELAND – NOVEMBER 25: LeBron James #23 of the Cleveland Cavaliers looks to pass off when double teamed by the Philadelphia 76ers November 25, 2006 at The Quicken Loans Arena in Cleveland, Ohio. Copyright 2006 NBAE (Photo by David Liam Kyle/NBAE via Getty Images)

James spent Thanksgiving weekend in 2006 on the other side of the Sixers-Cavaliers matchup.

On Nov. 25, 2006, a 21-year-old James recorded 25 points, 11 assists, four rebounds and one block in Cleveland's 108-95 win over Philadelphia.

Donning the Cavs' old-school orange threads, he played nearly 41 minutes.

Iverson led the Sixers with 31 points. Andre Iguodala added 17 points and eight rebounds, while Kyle Korver made three three-pointers off the bench.

James recorded 11 assists that night. Nearly 20 years later, another 11-assist performance against Indiana moved him past Jason Kidd for third place in NBA history.

The 2006 meeting also came near the end of Iverson's original run with Philadelphia. The Sixers traded him to Denver less than a month later.

James was 21. Iverson was nearing his departure.

Twenty years later, James is wearing a Sixers uniform and Iverson's No. 3 hangs above his home floor.

#2661. Why Is Arteta Acting Surprised?

A manager who is being disingenuous or one who starts to believe his own narrative?

Mikel Arteta is correct to point out that in the last couple of games Arsenal have dropped points because of not being clinical enough in front of goal, as well as decision-making in the final third.

It's the same reason the Gunners are no longer even in the Carabao Cup, because even against League Two opponents, a lack of firepower was costly.

Didn't the Spaniard himself stress after the Champions League final that improving the attack was the next step in getting over the line in Europe?

Under UEFA's current format (which is nonsense, by the way), a club can get away with a lack of offensive weapons. Yet in a knockout tie, the difference between progression and elimination is so small. It can be decided by who has that player who can produce a moment of magic out of nothing.

Andrea Berta's solution to improving the squad's front line was a bizarre one… allowing Trossard, Martinelli and Jesus to leave, along with Nwaneri (on loan), and replacing them with Tzolis.

Even from a maths point of view, if four men exit North London and only one arrives, that's clearly leaving the team with fewer alternatives.

It's not like his employers didn't make some serious money to afford to do more. You assume Mikel Arteta has enough power at the Emirates to have objected, so possibly didn't object enough.

Yet a team not converting opportunities or a recruitment strategy backfiring is part of the sport.

Why, though, is the man in charge now acting shocked over a reality many could have told him in the summer would happen?

Some Gooners think the definition of a supporter is that you can never be critical about the badge you love, so they will always defend strikers not scoring or midfielders not creating.

Yet there was a section of the fanbase jumping up and down, waving their arms, pleading with the boss not to stand still in a position of strength.

The 44-year-old is insulting those fans' intelligence by trying to act like he's now shocked and no one could see this coming.

Yes, he's the one who sees individuals daily in training, but he had evidence last season that makes you wonder what he thought would change.

He clearly still doesn't trust Gyökeres, at 27 Kai Havertz isn't suddenly going to score 20 league goals each campaign, and how many times does Madueke have to get his final ball wrong for you to accept it's not a coincidence?

Some of my peers are not innocent either.

Many prefer what we have to Vinícius Jr because apparently being nice is more important than who's better at football.

Noses have also been put up at Alvarez and Nico Williams. I even read during the World Cup that a fan wouldn't want Mbappé!!!!

The very same men and women who wrote this are now equally acting stunned that it turns out if you take away four members of a title-winning attack for someone from the Belgian top flight, your attack doesn't get better!

Yet, to be fair to those fans, this isn't their job. They are not getting paid a reported £20 million a year!

Anyone else notice those who are part of the recruitment process care about value for money but make sure they are well paid themselves?

Part of management is risk assessment. The easiest solution to a problem is de-escalation before the issue happens.

It's not acceptable to not listen to others who are telling you something negative is about to happen, then, when it happens, go into a monologue about the exact thing you were warned would occur.

Gooners, is Dan right that Arteta should have anticipated Arsenal's attacking problems during the summer, or is it unfair to blame the manager for the team's recent lack of clinical finishing?

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2657. How the Miami Heat saved the season after a terrible start

The Miami Heat ended last season in an awkward spot. For the fourth straight year, they found themselves in the NBA Play-In Tournament. Unfortunately, this was the first time they couldn't make it out. They have a S-Tier leading man calling the shots, a battle-tested defensive anchor, and a culture of winning in the ugliest ways possible.

Their roster, while nothing special, was far from the dregs of the association. It contained a good blend of young bucks and proven veterans. If the injury gods smiled in their favor and a couple of prospects took meaningful steps forward, the Heat could have run it back and flirted with 50 wins. And with their knack for upsets, maybe a postseason series victory would have followed.

However, the Heat, like the Minnesota Timberwolves, remembered that they didn't come to the table to nickel and dime their way through the nights. In Miami, they play for keeps. Win big, or go bankrupt trying. So, when Giannis Antetokounmpo finally became available, the Heat swung for the fences – trading the farm in the hopes that the singular excellence of the former two-time MVP, coupled with Bam Adebayo and the scrapes that remained would be enough to vault the team into true contention.

Through nine games, it looked like they would be filing for Chapter 7. The Heat were 3-6 and floundering, while their contemporaries (the Detroit Pistons, Boston Celtics, and Philadelphia 76ers) were thriving out the gate. But fast forward to today, and it looks like the big bet they placed may have been the right call.

After their 10-point win over the depleted Oklahoma City Thunder, the Heat are winners of their last seven games and now sit at No. 6 in the Eastern Conference – fully within striking distance of the conference's upper echelon.

In a team sport like basketball, it's foolish to point to one variable as the reason for positive change, as so many factors contribute to success, but it is hard not to watch this team and look at the ring leader as the catalyst: Erik Spoelstra.

Spoelstra may be the best coach in basketball. Heck, he may be one of the five best coaches that ever lived (we know he's at least one of the top 15). Spoelstra is innovative enough to turn oranges into lemonade. No, that's not a typo that was missed by my editor. The creative lens Spoelstra is able to analyze the game through literally defies everything we know about the human experience.

With an average age of 28.8 years old, the Heat have the second-oldest team in the NBA (behind only the Golden State Warriors). That is bad news bears in today's game – one that rewards athleticism, pace, and physicality. Spoelstra realized it was time to demote the veterans that most coaches would remain beholden too.

His biggest change was taking Andrew Wiggins (31 years old), and putting Pelle Larsson in his place (25). And when he's been hurt, instead of reverting back to Wiggins, Spoelstra simply plugs in Myron Gardner (25) in his place. A former second rounder and undrafted player in the place of a former first overall pick, NBA champion, and the third-highest paid player on the team's payroll.

Wiggins wasn't the only casualty. Bobby Portis' minutes are down, and Tim Hardaway Jr. is basically out of the rotation entirely. Along with Larsson and Gardner, those minutes are being eaten up by the youthful vigor of second round rookie Ryan Conwell (22). Despite hearing 36 names called before his on draft night, Conwell is seventh among rookies in minutes per game (26.2) in their last seven games.

Delegating hustle duties to fresher legs lessens the burdens on Antetokounmpo, Adebayo, Klay Thompson, and Davion Mitchell's shoulders, and enables them to focus more energy on scoring the ball. The Heat's effective field goal percentage is up 4.8% over the last seven games.

Spoelstra has also made a key strategic shift. To start the season, the Heat were doing a lot of hard hedging with ball screens involving their bigs. The idea is that since they start two center-sized players, they could afford for one of them to play these actions more aggressively, since the other one would be there to clean it up.

The idea wasn't a bad one, in theory, but playing this way asks the three guys not involved in the action to do a lot of flying around to cover up the gaps. Antetokounmpo, now in Year 14, has a lot of tread on his tires, and scrambling around possession after possession isn't necessarily high on his list of priorities.

So, instead of trying to fit a square peg into a round hole, Spoelstra scrapped the idea and started switching everything (except actions involving Portis, which the Heat continue to hedge). This asks Antetokounmpo and company to do a lot less rotating around, and it still lets the Heat benefit from their twin tower configuration (when one of them is switched onto the perimeter, the other can still lurk around the painted area).

As a result, the Heat are forcing fewer turnovers (the tradeoff of playing a less aggressive style). However, by switching everything, it is easier for them to keep the ball in front of them, and so the Heat's opponents are shooting far worse from the floor than they were before. And again, it conserves more energy, so the Heat have their legs under them on their own shots.

Due to the constraints of the written medium, we can't dissect ALL of Spoelstra's game-changing tweaks, but here are a couple of other developments you can see his fingerprint on: convincing Antetokounmpo into operating more off-the-ball, squeezing the last ounce of magic out of Thompson, and gradually helping mold Mitchell from bust to baller.

The good news for the Heat is that there are some aspects that will improve with time. Despite rostering Antetokounmpo and Adebayo – who have 11 All-Defensive Teams between the two of them – Miami is currently 24th in defensive rating.

The adjustments the Heat have made with minute allocation and scheme have helped bump them from 26th in this category in their first nine games to 17th in the last seven, but they are still being hurt by some bad luck.

This season, the Heat are surrendering a whopping 45.6% on wide open threes (per NBA.com). That is 2.7% than the next highest team, and 6.1% higher than the league average. The Heat under Spoelstra tend to give up more threes in order to prioritize protecting the rim, but defense has nothing to do with how well opponents shoot on open looks. That's just luck. If/when that number regresses to the mean (no team has allowed higher than 43% on these shots for an entire season), Miami's defensive rating will automatically improve.

Unfortunately, the Heat have also been the beneficiary of some good luck. According to Estimated Plus-Minus, they have had the third-easiest strength of schedule. They have also lost the fourth-fewest dollars to player injuries (per Spotrac). Antetokounmpo and Thompson have only missed one game each. Mitchell and Adebayo have been available for every game. What happens if one or two of those guys is out for an extended stretch? This isn't a super deep team.

More than likely, the conflicting noise between their negative shooting luck and positive schedule/injury history thus far is a wash. To me, the pace this Heat are currently on (51 wins) seems about right. They are a good team that, even with Spoelstra's magic touch, still has some glaring flaws (on-ball creation, offensive variety, depth) in a conference filled with them.

If they draw the first round opponent or injuries cause them to fall into the play-in tournament for the fifth straight year, another early exit could be in their future. But if Spoelstra keeps putting on a coaching clinic in the best league on the planet and Antetokounmpo can stay healthy enough to match him for a whole postseason, maybe, just maybe, the Heat can return to the NBA Finals for the first time since 2023.

The United States – the most successful nation in the history of the Davis Cup – are not present at the 2026 Davis Cup Finals.

Match One: Learner Tien defeated Jakub Mensik, 6-2, 6-4

Match Three: Christian Harrison and Austin Krajicek defeated Adam Pavlasek and Patrik Rikl, 5-7, 6-3, 10-8
