#2622. Landry Shamet has arrived. Why can’t he be Sixth Man of the Year?

Chicken Littles can relax. Our world champion Knicks are 11–6, sit fourth in the Eastern Conference, and have won eight of their last 10 games, including five straight. Karl-Anthony Towns is having an MVP-caliber season, and Captain Jalen Brunson is warming up after a short, celebration-heavy offseason. Another player who's getting some buzz isn't one of the starters, but the team's sharpest weapon off the bench.

When asked about Landry Shamet's play this season, head coach Mike Brown said the 6'5" guard "should be Sixth Man of the Year. It's not close." Mike should know. He has a front-row seat to the Shamet show every night and at every practice.

One stat I take note of is Game Score. John Hollinger designed it to measure a player's box-score production in a single game. Game Score uses a scale that roughly resembles points scored, with 10 considered an average performance and 40 an outstanding one. It rewards scoring, made field goals, rebounds, assists, steals, and blocks. Shot attempts, missed free throws, turnovers, and personal fouls subtract from the total, and offensive rebounds count more than defensive rebounds.

Through 17 games, Shamet has averaged a Game Score of 8.24. That puts him fourth on the team behind Towns (19.83), Brunson (18.66), and OG Anunoby (11.57). Two starters, Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges, rank fifth and sixth at 6.35 and 5.94, respectively.

This season has been a coming out party for Landry. Although primarily a linchpin of the second unit, he has filled in for starters five times this campaign and is averaging 26.9 minutes per game, the second-most of his NBA career. Consider these statistics, all career-best:

11.4 points per game, fourth-best on the team

The only Knick shooting better from deep is Jordan Clarkson (50%), coincidentally the 2020–21 Sixth Man of the Year. And Jordan's attempted only 12 longballs.

When Hart and Bridges have struggled to find the net, plenty of people have beaten the drum for Shamet to replace one of them in the first five. That sounds fine in theory, but consider Mike Brown's perspective. First, there's the harmony of keeping the Villanova brethren together, and who knows what effect a "demotion" for Josh or Kal might have on the locker room? Second, Shamet is Mike's security blanket. If the starters are spinning their wheels, nothing injects energy into the festivities like a Landry pull-up three on the move. The MSG crowd explodes, and you can see his teammates quicken with excitement. Furthermore, Shamet is doing much of his damage against the opponent's backups. That's hardly a fair fight. AND when the score is close and the team needs a bucket, Brown can turn to Captain Clutch, Towns, and his sparkplug Shamet. Even if Landry doesn't start, he sure can finish.

One downer about Landry's success is the ripple effect on the roster. Overshadowed by Shamet's sizzling shooting is the fact that Miles McBride is also shooting a career high from downtown (42%). Deuce was once a first-off-the-bench candidate. Now, with Shamet hitting the three-ball and Tyler Kolek coming into his own as a playmaker (averaging 4.1 assists to 0.6 turnovers in 13.3 minutes per game), McBride is down to 17.2 minutes per night, the fourth-highest average of his six-season career. Meanwhile, the Knicks find themselves dreadfully thin at center, with Andre Drummond losing the plot around the 10-minute mark most nights and James Wiseman yet to prove he can hang. Shamet + Kolek + Drummond + Wiseman = an expendable Deuce. No one here will be surprised if McBride, the longest-tenured Knick, is traded before the deadline for a serviceable big man. No, we won't like it, but we'll understand it.

Consider this: only three Knicks have won Sixth Man of the Year.

Why can't ShamWow be the fourth? He'll have some stiff competition in the race. Boston's Payton Pritchard is the current betting favorite for Sixth Man of the Year (+160 at BetMGM). That vanilla Milk Dud averages 13.7 points per game. Other top contenders include Ajay Mitchell (Thunder), Dylan Harper (Spurs), Jrue Holiday (Blazers), and Ayo Dosunmu (Timberwolves). Jared McCain and Daniss Jenkins are dark horses.

The stats make Landry a strong candidate, though. Through Nov. 22, Shamet ranked fifth in the NBA in on/off net rating among 242 qualifying players on HoopsNightly's leaderboard. The Knicks outscored opponents by 17.2 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor and were outscored by 8.3 with him off it. That's a swing of +25.5. (KnickStats gives him an even better number, +28.)

There used to be two knocks on Shamet, now in his ninth season. The first was that his defense stunk. Well, whattayaknow: according to KnickStats, the Knicks have allowed 101.3 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor and 117.5 with him off it. The other concern was the injury bug. He's missed significant time with lower-body issues, including multiple ankle sprains, a foot injury that kept him out for an extended stretch in 2023, and a calf strain that ended his 2023–24 season. Then came the right-shoulder setbacks, a dislocation in the 2024 preseason and a sprain in 2025 that sidelined him for roughly a month. For now (no jinxes), he's been the picture of health, playing every game of the campaign (we all wince whenever he smashes to the floor).

Everything's good until it isn't again. So it goes. For now, the Knicks are surging and tonight they'll face a familiar rival in the Cleveland Cavaliers. If you saw the injury report, it's a little dicey. Anunoby and Clarkson are out, while Hart, McBride, and Towns are all game-time decisions. That's a concerning list at first blush, but with sixth man Shamet in their back pocket, the Knicks still have a good chance to win their sixth straight. What a time to be a fan.

#2613. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2610. Matisse Thybulle Is the Lakers’ Secret Weapon

One of the biggest keys to the Lakers' stupendous 15-3 start has been defensive standout Matisse Thybulle.

The Lakers acquired Thybulle over last offseason on a $3.3 million deal. So far, he has been worth every penny.

Eighteen games in, the Lakers are hovering near the top 10 in defensive rating, thanks in part to them ranking first in steals per game and second in blocks.

A large part of their success on that end of the floor is Thybulle's defensive prowess.

Against the Charlotte Hornets on Nov. 17, Thybulle's defense helped L.A. win in overtime. With 11.5 seconds left in the game, the Lakers led 117-114. Hornets guard Royce O'Neale tried to inbound the ball when Thybulle flew in for a deflection that sealed the victory.

On a night when Quentin Grimes exploded for 47 points, Thybulle was the unsung hero. Making big defensive plays is nothing new for the former Naismith Defensive Player of the Year.

He ranks second in steals per game in the NBA (among those who have played at least five games), and boasts the most games with at least two steals and one block. He is on pace to be the first Laker ever to average two steals and a block for a season.

Thybulle's defensive tendencies impressed his teammates before the season even started. Back in training camp, rookie Cameron Carr named Matisse as the player who stood out the most, touting his defense as "ridiculous." With each game, Thybulle has continued to amaze.

"Honestly, he has those instincts of getting to the ball; it's like 'What, how did he get there?'" said teammate Collin Sexton. "So I think just being out there with him, you have to communicate with him; sometimes he communicates with you as well, like, 'I got it. I'm gonna get the steal,' and he goes out there and does it. He's one of those players that has great instincts, but also can read the game before it happens on the defensive side, so it's cool to be out there."

Just as a coach gives star players the green light offensively, the same can be true for the defensive end. Thybulle's knack for jumping passing lanes and getting in gaps earns him more trust from coaches to take risks.

"It's no different than a highly unique offensive player and giving them freedom to be creative; you've got to be able to do it within our system," Redick said. "He's got the freedom to be himself, and we know he's going to make more good happen than bad."

A major part of Thybulle's resounding impact on the Lakers isn't just his defense; it is also his offense.

The 29-year-old got off to a slow start offensively this season; however, he has since found a rhythm. He is shooting 40.5% from three on the highest attempts of his career — 4.4. Injuries have previously hindered his playing time at his previous stop in Portland, where he played a combined 45 games over the last two seasons.

Thybulle has started all 18 games for the Lakers, and joins former Defensive Player of the Year Victor Wembanyama as the only players to rack up at least 15 blocks, 20 steals and 30 threes this season. The Spurs and Lakers are tied for the best record in the league, and will square off Friday for the first time this season.

Many thought the Lakers took a risk in signing Thybulle over the summer.

But just as he continues to prove on the basketball court, some gambles are worth taking. And he was a steal.

#2605. Will Whitt Newbauer or Bowe Bentley be Oklahoma's starting QB in 2027?

The Oklahoma Sooners will have a major position to fill on their offense next football season. The Sooners will be one of many teams looking for a new starting quarterback.

Current starter, John Mateer, has had a stellar career. He's thrown for 8,713 yards, 64 touchdowns and 27 interceptions, while rushing for 1,744 yards and 28 scores. Mateer has been backed up by Whitt Newbauer and Bowe Bentley this season. Newbauer has played sparingly in Norman, completing just 3-of-5 passes for 12 yards in two seasons. He came after one season at Mercer, completing 56.4% of his passes for 1,398 yards, 12 touchdowns and four picks. Bentley is a true freshman, but was a top-10 quarterback in the 2026 class.

Head coach Brent Venables said both guys will get the chance at starting next season.

"Certainly there's a chance for that," Venables said. "They've had a good offseason, in the season. You get the practice reps that they share. We've tried to take some things off of John over the course of the week, just to be smart with his arm. They've been able to, a couple of times a week, get even more reps than what they'd normally get."

Venables' comments indicate that Oklahoma is already working to prepare both quarterbacks for a larger role. The additional practice reps should help them develop while giving the coaching staff a better look at what each can bring to the position. Replacing a quarterback with Mateer's production will be a big challenge, but the Sooners have two young options who will have an opportunity to make their case when the competition begins.

#2604. How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Wolves

Game 7 of the Western Conference Semifinals against the Sacramento Kings. My dad was in the family room, having what looked to be some kind of religious experience. 13-year-old me walked in, alarmed and… concerned? He had always been a bit of a curmudgeon, and now here he was, dancing in front of the TV, on the verge of bursting into a full-blown "Sister Act" number. I had never seen this side of him before. Whatever had my dad so enraptured seemed like something I'd like to be a part of myself.

"I'll have what he's having," essentially.

In that game, the Big Ticket, Kevin Garnett, would put up a godly stat line of 32 points, 21 boards, five blocks, and four steals, leading the Minnesota Timberwolves over the Kings with a final score of 83-80. It was pandemonium in the Dooley household.

May 19th, 2004, was the date that I was baptized and purified in the waters of Wolves basketball.

They'd go on to play the Los Angeles Lakers in the Western Conference Finals, and all I really remember from that series was Game 6, with the Wolves down 2-3. My dad and I drove over to my grandma's house off Lake Nokomis in South Minneapolis for a Monday visit and to anxiously watch the most important game of the season.

In my grandma's living room, I sank helplessly in her old reclining sofa chair as Kareem "not Abdul-Jabbar" Rush came off the bench and unconsciously fired away haymaker after haymaker from deep. The man they called K-Rush would hit his first six threes before finally missing late in the fourth when the damage had already been done.

In just six games, the Wolves were sent packing by a relative no-name on a roster full of future Hall of Famers. As someone new to the sport, even I knew that this was almost certainly not on the scouting report. Little did I know at the time, though, that the K-Rushes of the league would turn out to be some of my favorite players. But that night at least, I found K-Rush to be a pretty big jerk.

After learning what it felt like to be punched in the gut by sports – and I must say, it didn't feel great – I was now impatiently waiting for the next season to kick off.

Actually, I was more than ready. The Wolves would be ready as well. I always loved a good story, and the Wolves' was a vengeance quest. They would return. And this time around, they would end up hoisting the trophy that, two weeks later, after the Detroit Pistons shellacked those no-good-dirty-rotten Lakers, I learned belonged to some dude named Larry O'Brien, former NBA commissioner and politician who, according to his Wikipedia page, "learned about politics at a young age."

That hardware was on my mind for the rest of the summer. "Hey, Patrick, wanna go to Sebastian Joe's with me and Sam?" Sorry, can't. Too busy thinking about the Larry O'Brien Trophy.

A female classmate of mine asked me if I wanted to be her boyfriend. After I had just learned about this huge summer event called the NBA draft? Sorry, Ali, I gotta study.

Before I knew it, summer had ended, fall was upon us, and the 2004-05 season was just around the corner. My first full season as a fan of the Minnesota Timberwolves.

The Minnesota Timberwolves join terrifying kids commercials as some of my worst nightmare fuel.

Your teenage years are hard enough as it is. I didn't make it any easier for myself.

I tuned into every game that '04-05 season, waiting for the good vibes to come, but they never did. The January 19th game in Los Angeles against the antagonistic Lakers was an especially nauseating experience. I lay in bed trying to multitask between half-sleeping and listening to Chad Hartman on the radio call. The lights remained on deep into the night. The game was a back-and-forth tilt, with neither team able to get any real separation.

In the end, though, my AM radio would taunt me with Hartman's defeated utterances underneath the static scratches, of missed shots on one end and made shots on the other. Neither were from the right team. It felt unjust. What did I do to deserve this?

Despite running it back, the Wolves just couldn't get over the hump that year, and by proxy, I felt like I couldn't either. This thing called "Wolves fandom" had me feeling sluggish and languid. Like that gut punch from Game 6 of the WCF, I was learning in real time what prolonged, sustained depression feels like. Every game had me on pins and needles. I'm pretty sure this was the year I developed insomnia. I started having frequent sleep paralysis episodes, and also some of the most bizarre nightmares you could imagine.

My dad and I attended the Wolves' final regular-season game that year against the San Antonio Spurs, a team that two months later would be crowned NBA champions. In perhaps their best showing of the season, the Wolves dominated, winning by 22 points.

Former Wolves project Ndudi Ebi had what, to this day, is still the worst airball I have ever seen on a three-point "attempt". He also brought the roof down with a ferocious dunk that had the whole backboard shaking. That was the joy of guys like that.

We were sitting in the lower level right behind the hoop, equal parts in awe and also concerned that we were about to bear witness to a Shaq-shattering-the-backboard moment. (Un)fortunately, that moment never came, and after the game had ended, we left the Target Center wondering what could have been. If they had just played like that all season, maybe things could've gone differently.

Trendy pre-season favorites to win it all, the Wolves missed the playoffs that year, only managing to go 44-38. The late great coach Flip Saunders was fired 51 games into the season, replaced by General Manager and very tall man Kevin McHale.

Little did I know that, over the next 14 years, when my age would double and my stubble would fully grow into a lumberjack beard, at least record-wise, 2005 would be the summit.

The years that followed were a fast, rocky descent down a black diamond, and I was a kid with two left skis, held together with duct tape and blind hope.

Wavering optimism in the circles of Hell, or the life of a Wolves fan.

Sometimes I felt I had made a terrible mistake.

I had unknowingly chained a handcuff I didn't even know I was wearing to a ball dribbled by jesters, malcontents, and egocentrics: Ricky Davis, Marko Jarić, future podcaster Rashad McCants, and some guy with two first names whose scoring was inexplicably halved (20.3 to 10.1) because, as I was starting to realize, the Wolves were a team that could never have nice things.

Dwane Casey was hired as head coach for the 2005-06 season, and then was disposed of a season and a half later. This team was a steaming pile of dung, and the joke was on me for locking myself in the barn, waiting for the heap to turn to roses.

Fast-forward to the summer of '08: "The Dark Knight" had just come out. I went to the Southdale theater to watch the blockbuster film my peers were touting as "the best movie ever", a performance by the late Heath Ledger that critics were lauding as "Oscar-worthy". They weren't wrong. It was quite transformative. I thought to myself, "This was the same guy who played that cowboy?"

Now, I never contemplated becoming the Joker. If it had been released a year earlier, however, I may have considered it.

The previous summer, Garnett had finally had enough and rather unceremoniously parted ways with the Wolves in a big "blockbuster" trade. Minnesota's return really only had two bright spots to note, the first obviously being Al "Big Al" Jefferson.

Defending dunk contest champion Gerald Green.

Under the tutelage of perpetually confused Randy Wittman, the 2007-08 Wolves would go 22-60. Make no mistake, they were god-awful. But during that season's all-star game festivities, something finally clicked for me.

At New Orleans Arena, Gerald Green participated in the Saturday night dunk contest to defend his title, ultimately going toe-to-toe with Dwight Howard, AKA "Superman". Green broke out all sorts of crazy dunks: the alley-oop windmill, a behind-the-backboard under-the-legs slam. But there was one dunk that I will never, ever forget.

The cupcake dunk had never been pulled off, let alone even attempted. It has still not been replicated, nor has anyone, to my knowledge, dared even try.

Though Green would go on to relinquish his title to Howard, that dunk was the talk of the night. And I truly believe the only reason he didn't get a perfect score on it was because the judges didn't see what we all saw.

And it got me thinking. On a rudderless team, both managed and saddled by an inept franchise, what else is there to see? What can I look for?

To start, I accepted the truth: this team wasn't winning anything anytime soon.

Now that actual expectations had been tabled, I could watch the Wolves without worrying about superfluous things like "the outcome of a game" or "where the Wolves sit in the standings". If they lost, well, that's okay. I expected them to. If they won, I was amused. I had even perfected my dad's patented half-smile.

I also became a more well-rounded basketball fan, always following a second team to supplement my thirst for promising development. After the Seattle SuperSonics moved to Oklahoma City in 2008, I started to follow the young upstart Thunder. Making the leap from 23 wins to 50 in just one year. As a Wolves fan, I could've felt envy, but instead I was like a proud stepfather. I was the fan that stepped up.

In 2012, when they made it all the way to the Finals only to lose to that villainous Miami Heat superteam, I took it personally. But it felt good to care. The stakes had never been higher. I could never feel that way about the Wolves, who were in a league of their own.

And I tried to see it all for what it was: just basketball. Like the Actor in Albert Camus' "The Myth of Sisyphus", I invested myself in the Wolves for two-ish hours every game night, and once the contest was over, it was back to business as usual. It was back to life as usual. I wouldn't let the Wolves define me. They wouldn't determine how I felt moving forward. Sometimes a game would end in heartbreaking fashion, and I would feel that tiny hammer starting to peck away at that thing in my chest. No. I would relent. I refuse to let it hurt.

Well, if I was built like this guy, this would have been way easier.

But eventually I had to interrogate something deep: Why did I start following this team in the first place?

I had chosen to attach myself to this team during some of the most formative years of my life. And despite the Wolves at times almost insisting that I leave them be, I could never.

My father has lived in Minneapolis his entire life. As have I. I guess you could say we are predisposed to Minnesota sports fandom. It's in our bloodstream. When I watched my father react so fervently to that epic Game 7 all those years ago, it felt like something I would like to share with him. Up to that point, we hadn't shared all that much.

That shared fandom extends far beyond the father-son bond. It's a communal thing. Minneapolis is Wolves territory. To have pride in them is just one of the ways I choose to have pride in my community, where I'm from and where I stay to this day.

In 2013, having just graduated from the University of St. Thomas, I discovered Canis Hoopus, another communal outlet for me to share my allegiance to Wolves basketball. That became a way for me to lean into the real truth I had been avoiding. Like it or not, the Wolves were now an integral part of me. And to ignore that part, to detach myself from it and let myself become jaded would, as Camus so bluntly put it, be a defeat of the human soul.

So, whether I was using Canis to spam the game threads with Free Dieng! or as an excuse to play around with iMovie, I was no longer afraid to let it all out. The Wolves were like an alley-oop, and I was Gerald Green, or Zach LaVine – take your pick; if there's one thing the Wolves have, it's dunk champs – and the team was all of us, together.

Not too long after Garnett was traded, another movie came out: "Into the Wild", adapted from the novel of the same name and the real-life story of Christopher McCandless, a naive, pretentious young college graduate who, left to his own devices, went on a solo hike across North America and into the Alaskan wilderness. Along the way, he made many friends, but ultimately always left them behind to continue his trek alone.

Eventually, he ate a berry that turned out to be poisonous. He would soon pass away in an abandoned bus in the wild, but not before writing in his journal a revelatory "Happiness is only real when shared."

While I find that a bit reductive, I believe that happiness is best when shared. And it's not just limited to happiness. As my former neighbor Dave Pirner once sang, "Misery loves company."

The highs and the lows, the celebratory and the funereal. All of it is best, and can be eased, by a shared camaraderie among people.

And that's how I learned to truly embrace the Wolves, by finding community in the struggle, and by finding myself in that communal openness where all mirrors are welcome, where the subjective woe can turn into a collective joy, and I am forever grateful for that.

Aaron Rodgers made his first public comments since being benched by the Steelers on The Pat McAfee Show on Wednesday afternoon and they were very critical of head coach Mike McCarthy.

Rodgers said he also believes McCarthy has lost the team in general.

“Everybody in that building knows the truth,” Rodgers said.

Rodgers said similar things happened when the two men were with the Packers and that he believes McCarthy blames him for being fired in Green Bay after the 2018 season. He said he saw that McCarthy was not connecting with Steelers players early in training camp, but tried to help smooth things out.

“I protected him,” Rodgers said. “I didn’t talk about the things publicly. I didn’t talk about his habits.”

Rodgers said that he told the team that if they weren’t going to make those alterations that they should release him and said that there was no chance of a reconciliation with the team after how they handled things on Tuesday.

#2599. Rob Pelinka believes the Lakers are feeding off Luka Dončić’s leadership

Behind Luka Dončić's wondrous play, which has thrust him into the center of early season MVP conversations, the Los Angeles Lakers are off to a roaring 15-3 start and tied for the West's No. 1 seed. Whether it's his elite self-creation, willingness to embrace more off-ball work, brilliant playmaking or growth on the defensive end, there are many on-court factors explaining why Dončić has been so impactful for Los Angeles this year.

But Lakers GM Rob Pelinka also believes Dončić's leadership is paramount to this team's success thus far. Pelinka deems Dončić's leadership as bred through plenty of personal experiences that have shaped him in recent years.

"Adversity in life is what makes us all grow and he's been through a lot. Getting traded, he's had some family stuff, making sure he can stay close to his daughters," Pelinka said prior to Friday's win over the Sacramento Kings. "That's all adversity and I've seen it really grow his character in the form of leadership just being able to go through some of that stuff that life throws all of us, it throws our way. The guys in the locker room feed off his leadership. The other thing I've really seen about Luka is he takes accountability. He has so many great games but if he has a down game, he looks around the guys, he's like, 'This one's on me. I've got to be better.' I think a great leader can recognize that and really have seen that growth in him this year."

Pelinka's mention of accountability was readily on display last week when the Lakers' nine-game winning streak came to a halt after they lost to the Utah Jazz. That night, Dončić scored 29 points on 10-of-28 shooting (2-of-12 from deep) and had seven assists to nine turnovers. Following the defeat, Dončić didn't mince words about his own play and refused to let the second leg of a back-to-back be any sort of excuse for the team's poor performance.

"I mean, honestly, I just got to be way better than this," Dončić told reporters. "This is unacceptable for my part. I've got to lead the team in better ways. I look at this game, got to move on and learn from this."

The Lakers will hope both Dončić's leadership and on-court splendor power them to a win Friday night when they face the San Antonio Spurs in a clash between 15-3 teams vying for the West's top spot.

#2598. Zac Taylor looks back on Bengals disappointing loss at Washington

Of the Cincinnati Bengals' three losses so far in 2026, the Nov. 23 loss to the Washington Commanders was really the one that got away.

The Bengals (7-3) were competitive in all three losses to varying degrees, but at Washington, they led most of the night, recaptured the lead with under a minute to play and couldn't get one final stop after that in a 22-20 walk-off field goal win for the Commanders (4-5-1).

Bengals Commanders Jason Williams Hey, Zac Taylor, Joe Burrow. What happened to running the ball?

Cincinnati has a short week to prepare for their Nov. 29 home game against the New Orleans Saints (3-7), but spent most of his Nov. 25 news conference at Paycor Stadium revisiting key aspects of the costly loss to the Commanders.

Following the Bengals' Sunday Night Football win over AFC North rival Pittsburgh on Nov. 15, one Bengals' captain essentially chalked up the state of the Bengals' running game to: "When we're passing it like we are, why force a running game."

That wasn't a bad way to think about the win over the Steelers, which the Bengals dominated. But at Northwest Stadium against Washington, Cincinnati amassed just 31 rushing yards. That sum flirted with the 23 yards they gained on the ground in the loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars on Oct. 4, which stands as the worst rushing game by the team under Taylor.

The working theory within the Bengals' offense has a few prongs related to the run game, and one was conveyed by the Bengals' captain. Another prong is that the Bengals have passing plays that essentially function as running plays using dump-offs around the line of scrimmage. And maybe those plays develop in ways that are more advantageous for Cincinnati's backs, Chase Brown and Samaje Perine.

The Bengals are going into Week 12, and Taylor seemed to say the Bengals are who they are when it comes to running the ball.

With that could come difficulties in games like the one they lost as Washington.

"I think 'Pitch' (offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher) said it best: 'We'll be whoever we need to be as the year goes on," Taylor said. "He said that in training camp and in the offseason. I still feel very strongly about that as the season goes."

On the stroke of the two-minute warning in the fourth quarter, the Bengals were perched on the Commanders' 33-yard line with a fresh set of downs following a 32-yard reception by Mike Gesicki.

From there, the go-ahead field goal by Evan McPherson would have been 50 yards, well within his makeable range. But the Bengals also had the game in their hands in every respect, and a further first down would move McPherson even closer for what could have been a walk-off field goal. That was the dream scenario, but it didn't come to fruition for several reasons.

There was an injury timeout that stopped the clock, but in what many would assume as a running situation, the Bengals had Burrow drop back to pass twice. First, he was almost intercepted. The second time, he was sacked, moving McPherson's eventual go-ahead kick back to 55 yards.

McPherson made the kick, but Washington got the ball back with enough time to move into range for its own walk-off field goal.

"It played out the same either way and I understand that was because of an injury timeout," Taylor said. "But the point is, I wanted to kick a field goal with three seconds left and win the game so you don't give them any opportunity to do what they just did.

"I felt very strongly putting the ball in (Burrow's) hands and throwing the ball and seeing if we can get the first down."

Of the Burrow sack on third down, Taylor said he could have given the offense a better chance at converting via his play-calling.

As ugly as Cincinnati's offense looked early on against Washington, the Commanders looked worse. A lot of that had to do with the Bengals getting to quarterback Jayden Daniels.

Boye Mafe tallied three sacks by himself, and the Bengals were really making life difficult for the Commanders at the line of scrimmage and in their backfield.

But then the pressure on Daniels disappeared. Washington's offense found a groove on its final drive of the first half, eventually scoring on each of its last six drives.

The Commanders' last five drives ended in field goals by kicker Drew Stevens — each from 41 yards and closer.

To the defense's credit, Washington had minimal success in the red zone and scored just one touchdown. And you might have liked Cincinnati's chances if you were told ahead of time Washington would only score 22 points in the game.

But the Bengals might need to win tight, low-scoring games like this down the road, and do so against higher-caliber opponents.

When Cincinnati could not longer get to Daniels, it also couldn't get off the field.

Taylor agreed some rotation along the defensive line could have helped but for what he called a strange start to the game, plus the fact that the defense was getting off the field for almost the entire first half.

"You've got to find some opportunities for Shemar (Stewart) and Cedric (Johnson) to mix it in… We'll rotate those guys a little more," Taylor said.

This article originally appeared on Cincinnati Enquirer: Zac Taylor looks back on Bengals disappointing loss at Washington

#2594. Scottie Barnes just passed this Raptors legend in points scored

After his last game, Scottie Barnes snagged the title of player with the seventh most points ever for the Toronto Raptors. Having already vaulted over Fred VanVleet and Jonas Valančiūnas earlier in his career to comfortably move up the top 10, Barnes has just passed Morris Peterson, who played seven years in Toronto in the 2000s.

Mo Pete was a Michigan State swingman who was drafted 21st overall in the 2000 NBA draft, and finished fourth in the rookie of the year race in his first season with the Raps. #2592. Chamblee Demands End To PGA Tour Safety Nets For LIV Returnees

Brandel Chamblee believes the PGA Tour must stop protecting players who left for the breakaway circuit. The analyst argues that returning golfers need to earn their spots through the same grueling path as everyone else. This stance comes as the tour prepares to split into two tiers for the 2028 season. The new structure will focus heavily on promotion and relegation to keep the field competitive. Chamblee insists that existing exemptions for former LIV members should vanish immediately. He sees the current system as a loophole that undermines the meritocratic nature of professional sports.

Speaking on The Big Swing with Jimmy Roberts, Chamblee outlined a harsh reality for stars like Bryson DeChambeau and Jon Rahm. Both men won major championships in the last three years and will likely face one-year suspensions before returning. Exemption for the Championship Series in 2028 would apply to them under current plans. Chamblee rejects this idea entirely. "I wouldn't be surprised if some of these players have got to go back to the Korn Ferry Tour, got to go to the [Challenger Series], and then work their way into the Championship Series, and as they should," he said. "You've got to come back and prove yourself." He argues that the tour has too many safety nets that let players stay at the highest level long after they have lost their edge.

Chamblee views the removal of these protections as essential for the health of the game. He believes the tour can easily get rid of these safety nets to create a fairer environment. "If you really want to make golf more meritocratic, you need to get rid of these safety nets," he told reporters. This approach contrasts sharply with the recent handling of players like Marco Penge, who nearly lost his card at The RSM Classic. Penge's victory at Sea Island secured his top-100 status and a spot on the Championship Series for 2028. After their major wins this season, Aaron Rai and Ryan Fox gained exemptions until the end of 2031. The difference in treatment between those who stayed and those who left is the core of Chamblee's argument.

The analyst also defended outgoing commissioner Jay Monahan against critics who blame him for the LIV Golf disruption. According to GolfMagic, Chamblee compared LIV's business model to a carmaker giving vehicles away for free. "The only thing that was unique about it [LIV] was it was a business model that did not care about their return on investment," Chamblee said. He noted that no one could have predicted an irrational actor entering the arena. "Well, no, because nobody could have foreseen an irrational actor coming into the arena. So, you know, I'm not quick to blame Jay Monahan," he added. Monahan will step down at the end of 2026, with Brian Rolapp taking over on January 1. Chamblee hopes history will be kind to Monahan given the unique challenges he faced.

Chamblee remains skeptical about the long-term value of the LIV Golf product. He argues that the circuit failed because it tried to manufacture passion without the element of national pride. "Well, it took some 70 years for the Ryder Cup to develop the passionate following that it had, but the players in the Ryder Cup are playing for their country," Chamblee said. He dismissed the idea that team golf could replicate that emotion. "LIV golfers were playing for greed and that was it." This financial motivation, he suggests, is why the breakaway could not sustain the same emotional connection as traditional team events.

Over the past four years, the analyst continues to worry about the harm done to the sport. "I think people look back and at least over the last 40 or 50 years, remember this is probably the worst period in golf's history and I'm not so sure that it won't echo unfortunately into the future," he added. Despite these bleak assessments, the focus now shifts to the 2027 season and the changes coming in 2028. The tour will likely see a more rigid structure where performance dictates status, and past contracts offer no shield from the qualifying process.

#2587. Week 12 Fantasy Football Rookie Stock Watch: Antonio Williams And Jonah Coleman Break Out While Others Struggle

Now that we have reached Week 12, we are beginning to figure out exactly who the 2026 rookie class is, at least when it comes to this season. Some have been playing great, while others have struggled. This is our fantasy football rookie stock watch, where we tell you whose stock is up and whose stock is down.

Coleman absolutely exploded in Week 11. He's been playing very well, but this was his true breakout game against the Las Vegas Raiders. On 24 carries, he rushed for 111 yards and three touchdowns, while catching four of five targets for 18 yards.

To make matters even better, JK Dobbins was just suspended by the Broncos for conduct detrimental to the team. As we predicted dating back to the summer, this backfield now belongs to Coleman, and he is going to be a league-winner.

Williams is another rookie who had his first true breakout game in Week 11. He did it in an upset win over the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday Night Football.

We had been waiting for him to explode since Terry McLaurin went down with a season-ending injury, and he came out and caught nine of 11 targets for 122 yards, including the game-sealing catch. His rest-of-season value is up, and his dynasty stock is now way up.

Price has now been back from injured reserve and on the field alongside Zach Charbonnet for three games, and it has not gone great. He is the clear secondary back to Charbonnet, and he even saw his targets disappear in Week 10 before the Seahawks' bye. There is a chance he takes over, but it's not looking good.

Our expectation is that you are going to get about 8-10 carries with a few targets in each game moving forward, and you won't be happy unless he falls into the end zone. That's a bad bet because he has scored one touchdown all season.

Douglas really struggled in Week 11, dropping multiple passes, including a potential touchdown. He finished the game catching just two of 10 targets for 30 yards. There is no doubt his stock is down.

However, we are here to tell you not to panic on Douglas, and even buy low if you get the chance. We love the targets and opportunities he saw, and based on what we've seen all year, this was just an outlier game.

#2585. Joe Brady can become the fifth coach ever to win 10 of his first 11 games

Buffalo’s Joe Brady is off to one of the best starts for any head coach in NFL history.

The Bills are 9-1, which means that if they beat the Chiefs on Thanksgiving night, Brady will be just the fifth coach in NFL history to win 10 of his first 11 games.

The four who have done it before are Jim Caldwell (11-0 with the 2009 Colts), Wally Lemm (who went 9-0 as interim head coach of the 1961 Houston Oilers and then won one of his first two games after becoming head coach of the 1962 St. Louis Cardinals), Steve Mariucci (10-1 with the 1997 49ers) and Red Miller (10-1 with the 1977 Broncos).

Brady took over a good Bills team and has kept them near the top of the NFL. His record to start his head-coaching career is impressive, but he was brought in to win in the postseason, and so it’s too soon to say whether the Bills’ decision to fire Sean McDermott and replace him with Brady will pay off.

#2582. 49ers QB Brock Purdy misses practice and is day to day with an ankle injury

SANTA CLARA, Calif. (AP) — San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy missed practice on Wednesday after hurting his ankle during last week's win against the Minnesota Vikings.

Coach Kyle Shanahan said that Purdy hurt himself in the second quarter of Sunday night's 35-10 win over the Minnesota Vikings but was able to remain in the game. He was not available for practice to begin the week of preparation for Sunday's division showdown against Seattle and is listed as day to day.

"He can't go today so it's always a possibility," Shanahan said if Purdy could miss the game against the Seahawks. "It's not a high ankle so it's day to day with it. We'll see how it goes."

Purdy is coming off a stellar performance against the Vikings after throwing for 255 yards and three touchdowns against one of the top defenses in the league to win NFC Offensive Player of the Week.

Purdy leads the NFL with 118.2 passer rating and 9.0 yards per pass attempt, to go with his 23 touchdown passes and only five interceptions.

Mac Jones handled the first-team work in practice on Wednesday. Jones started eight games last season when Purdy was sidelined by turf toe and helped San Francisco post a 5-3 record during that time.

Receiver Mike Evans also sat out of practice on Wednesday as the 49ers are managing the Achilles tendinitis that sidelined him for three games. Linebacker Dre Greenlaw (neck), receiver Jordan Watkins (groin), and defensive back Siran Neal (knee, foot) also didn't practice.

Defensive backs Deommodore Lenoir (foot) and Upton Stout (shoulder), and offensive linemen Austen Pleasants (knee) and Carver Willis (illness) were limited. Pleasants had his 21-day practice window opened Wednesday after starting the season on injured reserve.

The 49ers also activated cornerback Nate Hobbs off the injured reserve list and placed right tackle Colton McKivitz on IR with a season-ending ankle injury. Receiver Brandin Cooks was re-signed to the practice squad after being cut last week.

Defensive end Nick Bosa said he wasn't surprised by the boos he got in Mexico City after his remarks last week about how they cheered.

Bosa was booed loudly when he was showed on the video board before the game on Sunday after saying the Mexican fans needed to be taught about how to cheer at NFL games. Bosa said he didn't want the fans to cheer constantly as they do in soccer but to reserve their loud chants to when Minnesota was on offense.

Bosa said his intentions were "pure" and he didn't mean to offense anyone but the local fans were upset and made him know about it. Bosa said he expected that reaction but enjoyed his overall trip.

"I thought it was good," he said. "I definitely didn't mean any harm with my comments. The environment was amazing like it was the last time I was there."

#2577. NBA plans to invest 10bn euros in European arenas

The NBA has stepped up its plans for a European league by announcing a strategy to invest at least 10bn euros in the development and renovation of basketball arenas across the continent.

The league has assembled a group of investment firms for the project, which would also look to improve the sports and entertainment districts around the arenas.

The initiative forms part of the NBA and the International Basketball Federation's (Fiba) plan to launch a new, professional basketball system in Europe in 2027.

It will provide prospective clubs and ownership groups with access to capital and the NBA's expertise in regard to developing modern arenas and their surroundings.

"We've seen first-hand how state-of-the-art arenas and the related developments around them can transform basketball teams and their surrounding communities," said NBA commissioner Adam Silver.

"As we prepare to launch a new league in Europe alongside Fiba, we see a significant opportunity to help clubs develop facilities which both build on the unique traditions that define European basketball while also elevating the fan experience and attracting many more live events."

The NBA's announcement stated that the plans for the areas surrounding arenas could include housing, workplaces, restaurants, retail and public spaces, ensuring they would be year-round destinations.

In the statement, the investors said: "We're excited to work with the NBA to support a transformative phase of infrastructure development across Europe.

"Together, we have the potential to invest billions of euros to create world-class venues in European cities, honouring the passion and traditions of European basketball fans and supporting lasting economic growth in the communities where the game means so much."

The announcement cited a study by The Sports Consultancy, which claimed the NBA and Fiba's league could contribute more than 24bn euros in gross value added to GDP across Europe.

It also claimed the league could support nearly 15,000 full-time equivalent jobs annually and attract nearly 70 million spectators over its first 10 years.

#2575. 'Sad to see:' Steelers players, NFL world weigh in on Aaron Rodgers breakup

Aaron Rodgers has long had a cannon for an arm. As it turns out, he also has a flamethrower for a mouth.

On Wednesday, the Rodgers-Pittsburgh Steelers era ended after the quarterback was released following his unceremonious benching on Nov. 24. Rodgers not only lost his starting gig, but also an active roster spot, a day after the team announced the passer would be inactive for the Week 12 Black Friday game vs. the Denver Broncos.

Prior to his release, Rodgers reaction to the benching wasn't the typical PR-talk reserved for veterans. Instead, the passer aired dirty laundry of the Steelers' inner workings underneath head coach Mike McCarthy on the Nov. 25 edition of the "Pat McAfee Show," highlighted by the fact that McCarthy would allegedly fall asleep in meetings or fail to attend them altogether.

Rodgers' release and subsequent accusations – which the quarterback says can be corroborated by a number of players on the team – drew plenty of reaction, skepticism and some verification from plenty around the NFL sphere.

Drew Allar, the rookie fourth-round pick of the Steelers, kept it amicable when discussing Rodgers, deciding not to weigh in on the release, instead wishing the passer the best in his future endeavors.

"For me, it's kind of sad to see, because I have a lot of respect for Aaron," Allar told reporters on Wednesday. "I've learned a lot from him since he's been here. I think, again, I'm just gonna leave it at that."

The tight end, who Rodgers says broke the news of his benching and deactivation to him on Wednesday, tried his best to keep questions related to the Steelers' upcoming matchup vs. the Denver Broncos on Black Friday.

"Like I said, I'm just gonna focus on answering questions on the Broncos and the game on Friday, I really have nothing to add," Freiermuth said when questioned about McCarthy's sleeping habits.

When asked about his conversation with Rodgers on the evening of Nov. 24, he added: "I was just checking in on a close friend from what I heard. That's all I have to say about that."

As for his level of confidence in McCarthy and the coaching staff?

Wilson, with whom Rodgers had a seemingly rocky playing relationship with during his tenure with the Jets, opted not to add fuel to the fire when asked about Rodgers' benching.

"I just worry about what's going on over here, man," Wilson said.

Ben DiNucci, who spent time with the Dallas Cowboys while McCarthy was head coach, weighed in on Rodgers' allegations, saying the head coach was present (and awake) during his time in Dallas.

The former Steelers safety, who spent eight seasons in Pittsburgh, kept it short on his reaction:

"Feel how you want, but word is.... "Not 1 lie told".," Clark posted on X.

#2573. Lakers star divulges ‘uncomfortable’ reason for success without Austin Reaves

For the first four weeks of the season, the Lakers, for the most part, won their games in similar fashion.

A scorching start from Luka Doncic en route to a 30-point (and oftentimes, 40-point) performance.

Austin Reaves, Doncic's backcourt co-star, efficiently filled in the gaps offensively en route to an uber-efficient 25-point game.

Walker Kessler provided the rim pressure the team needed, which in combination with the scoring/playmaking from Doncic and Reaves, opened up scoring opportunities for the players around them.

Luka Doncic #77 and Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers look on. NBAE via Getty Images

Los Angeles Lakers forward Jarred Vanderbilt playing defense. AP Photo/Kyusung Gong

The recipe not only led to the Lakers winning 12 of their first 14 games, but also powered them to have the league's top-ranked offense.

But then the formula that led them to most of their early-season victories changed before their longest stretch of games at home.

The ingredients changing meant the recipe for success also had to be altered – which the Lakers successfully pulled off during the 3–1 homestand that ended with Monday's victory over the Jazz.

Doncic cooled off from his sizzling start to the season during the homestand, averaging 29.5 points (38.5% shooting, 23.5% on 3-pointers), after averaging 39 points (48.6% shooting, 40.6% on 3s) beforehand.

Utah Jazz forward Kyle Filipowski (2) goes up for a basket as Los Angeles Lakers center Walker Kessler (14) defends. AP Photo/Kyusung Gong

Reaves wasn't available, missing the last five games because of a bruised left heel. The Lakers are hopeful he'll return during Friday's road game against the Spurs.

Which led to the Lakers leaning on their defense to pull out most of their recent wins.

"We have a standard and we have to play to that standard and do what we're supposed to," Collin Sexton said. "When you're playing to a standard, it doesn't matter who's in and who's out. We all have to help. It doesn't matter who's coming into the game, we all have a role to play to do what the person in front of us did."

The Lakers held the Hornets to 114 points in their overtime win Nov. 17, allowed 109 points in the Nov. 18 loss to the Jazz, held the Kings to 104 points in Friday's win before holding the Jazz to 94 points on Monday, which is the fewest amount of points a team has scored against the Lakers this season.

Los Angeles Lakers forward Jarred Vanderbilt (2) vies for the ball against Utah Jazz forward Kyle Filipowski. AP Photo/Kyusung Gong

Their halfcourt defense has been a strength of the Lakers throughout the season.

But they cleaned up some of their transition defensive concerns. They remained disruptive, recording at least 16 turnovers in each game of the homestand. And using more zone defense, sometimes with full-court pressure, gave the Lakers a boost on that end of the floor.

"We have a lot of like disruptors defensively," Jake LaRavia said. "We do a good job at just creating pressure for the other team, whether it's deflections or just ball pressure, and kind of making them uncomfortable in bringing the ball up the court. It's obviously been working for us, so we're going to keep doing it 'til it stops working."

The Lakers' defensive rating improved from No. 17 to No. 10 during the homestand – albeit against inferior opponents that have a combined record of 9–43.

They're going to need Reaves available and improved play from Doncic as the level of competition picks up with the four-game trip post-Thanksgiving that features matchups against the Spurs, Grizzlies and Rockets. Those are three of the four teams closest to the Lakers in the top of the Western Conference standings.

#2561. Aaron Rodgers rips Mike McCarthy, says coach fell asleep in meeting, mistakenly called team 'Packers'; league sources reportedly corroborate Rodgers' account

Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers did not stay silent for long following his surprise benching, which was announced by the team on Tuesday night.

The four-time NFL MVP joined the "Pat McAfee Show" on Wednesday afternoon to address his benching … and he did not hold back when it came to sharing his side of how the events of the week unfolded — or when it comes to his feelings about head coach Mike McCarthy.

"I found out that I was gonna be inactive on a phone call last night from Pat Freiermuth," Rodgers said in the interview. "I was talking to Muth and a couple of the guys, and he said, 'I can't believe they're doing this.' And I said, 'Doing what?' I didn't know. And he told me, and obviously, there had been a lot of things in motion at that point. I didn't hear from Mike [McCarthy]."

"Mike and I talked for a long time the last few days, and that word [benching] never came up," Rodgers continued.

After that, Rodgers released a windfall of scathing accusations against McCarthy, ripping into his head coach for a series of events over the past week that "ultimately led to where we're at now."

Rodgers said McCarthy arrived late to a quarterbacks meeting last Wednesday, in which the coach fell asleep and was snoring. Rodgers accused McCarthy of missing an offensive meeting the following day and also missed the Friday walkthrough.

"Doesn't come to the first walkthrough," Rodgers said. "Doesn't come to the protection walkthrough on Thursday. Saturday, he misses the morning meeting, and we don't have a team meeting Saturday night for whatever reason in Philly. And then comes Sunday, when obviously we struggled, and the product wasn't great."

Rodgers also ripped into McCarthy's relationships with players on the team, alleging that he didn't care to get to know the defense and had lost many of those players well before the end.

"There were some guys early on that were … didn't like the way things were going, especially defensive guys. Mike didn't want to get to know the defense," Rodgers said. "At one point, I told him, 'You should really lean into the defensive guys a little bit more and talk to those guys,' and he said, 'Well, I don't think I need to.' And I said, 'Well, I disagree with that.'"

"He already kind of lost a lot of those guys, and I think the nail in the coffin for so many of us was, at halftime, toward the end of it … he says, 'Alright, 1-2-3-Packers!' That's what he broke it down on in the locker room," Rodgers said. "We all looked around, going, 'What the f***? What is going on? Where's his head at, at this point?"

The Steelers went on to lose that game, 19-16, snapping a seven-game losing streak for the Philadelphia Eagles. Rodgers took five sacks in the loss, completing 30-of-44 pass attempts for 227 yards and a score.

Clearly, the loss was a tipping point for Rodgers.

"I went in on Monday, and I just said, "Hey, this last week, this is not what we talked about. We've had these conversations for months now. And it began as a concerned friend about somebody who's unhealthy. If you're sleeping in meetings, you're unhealthy. If you're not coming to everything you should be coming to as a playcaller, [you're unhealthy].

"I mean, how many quarterbacks around the league are dealing with the same type of stuff? I gave you one week. I could go week-by-week throughout the season on stuff that was going on.

"Monday, we're having this conversation, and I said, 'We need to make a change for the betterment of the team.'"

The change Rodgers was hoping for was a change in playcaller. But instead, the team made a change at quarterback.

How do Aaron Rodgers and the Steelers move forward after this?

Well … apparently, they don't. Rodgers acknowledged as much nearing the end of his McAfee appearance, saying the "ship has sailed" on a return to the team.

Soon after Rodgers' interview concluded, it was reported that the Steelers were releasing Rodgers, according to Pittsburgh Post-Gazette beat writer Gerry Dulac. Other reports have since confirmed the same.

The real question now is how the Steelers will move forward with McCarthy, after multiple league sources have corroborated Rodgers' account to ESPN, their team reports.

Skies are Gray but things are looking Sonny!Welcome back, Sonny Gray! pic.twitter.com/Ky2sBhVi57

Gray, 37, finished fifth in the American League Cy Young voting this season after throwing 169 innings with a 2.72 ERA and strong underlying numbers for the Boston Red Sox. He was the AL Cy Young runner-up in 2023, his final season with the Twins. All told, Gray threw 303 ⅔ innings with a 2.90 ERA during his time in Minnesota.

CBS Sports ranked Gray as the No. 14 free agent available on the market this offseason. Here's our write-up:

Gray has reportedly mulled retirement over the last few offseasons, but he intends to pitch in 2027. He's as crafty as ever, using six pitches regularly and giving hitters every look. Hard, soft, sharp break, big movement, etc. Gray's stuff works in such a way that he seems to get a quick first or second pitch out every inning, allowing him to pitch deep into games. He completed six innings 22 times in his 29 starts this past season, which makes him a workhorse by 2026 standards. Gray will pitch the entire 2027 season at age 37 and he's lost enough velocity to shrink his margin of error meaningfully, which creates some over-the-cliff risk. Still, the 14-year veteran is not out of place as the No. 2 starter in a postseason rotation.

Gray now joins a Twins rotation that includes Taj Bradley, Joe Ryan and Pablo López, who missed last season after undergoing Tommy John surgery in February. Other options include Dean Kremer, Bailey Ober and Mick Abel.

The Twins are coming off a 2026 season in which they went 77-85 with a -58 run differential. That landed them in third place in the American League Central and seven games out of the third and final wild-card spot in the AL. Although the Twins improved upon their 2025 record, they've now missed the postseason for three straight years, their longest drought in a decade. The Gray addition -- plus catcher Ryan Jeffers' acceptance of the qualifying offer for 2027 -- helps the cause, and no doubt the Twins under second-year manager Derek Shelton will be looking to get back to the playoffs in what again figures to be a winnable division.

#2555. Rob Manfred 'can't imagine' MLB team owners will accept new CBA without a salary cap

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball commissioner Rob Manfred on Wednesday said club owners are not willing to compromise on their push for a salary cap and floor in their ongoing negotiations with the players union on a new collective bargaining agreement. While Manfred noted there was general room for compromise with the MLBPA, that does not extend to the central matter of the capped system owners want.

"I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," Manfred said while meeting with the press during the ongoing owners meetings in New York, via the Athletic.

"Thirty clubs are 100% unanimous in support of the proposals that have been made," Manfred said later during a news conference at MLB headquarters. "I'm not in a position to speculate about what happens in the event that we don't achieve our overriding objective, which is to get a cap and floor system that addresses the competitive problem that our fans perceive."

It's possible to parse "can't imagine" as a subtle rhetorical hedge. Additionally, Manfred before he was commissioner was the league's lead negotiator. As such, he's quite familiar with the appearance of unyielding resolve as a tactical implement. Thus, the league has tied every other proposed change to the players' acceptance of a cap and floor, and the players through their union have historically shown zero willingness to accept such a system.

"There can be no clearer example of the league's lack of seriousness than their insistence that they will not negotiate over the economics outside of a radical change to the system that would dramatically reduce overall player compensation for all categories of players and strip fundamental rights from players like the ability to have truly guaranteed contracts," MLBPA interim head Bruce Meyer said Wednesday in a statement.

"There should be no illusions about the owners' true motivation in pushing for this system. They want to make more money in profits and franchise values by artificially suppressing player salaries."

In their most recent substantive proposal to the players, MLB pitched a $258.3 million cap and $180.2 million floor on team payrolls, with those limits to be phased in gradually. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor.

The current CBA, which is the accord that governs every aspect of the working relationship between players and clubs in MLB, is set to expire just before midnight on Dec. 1. At that point, the league is expected to lock out the players at the behest of team owners. The lockout will likely not end until a new CBA is agreed to, at least in principle. Owners also locked out the players in 2021, and that lockout lasted 99 days and very nearly ate into the 2022 regular-season schedule.

#2554. Sean McVay on Puka Nacua: 'Can't say for certain' what his Rams future will be amid pending free agency

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua is likely out for the remainder of the season after undergoing surgery for an MCL injury he sustained on the final offensive snap of the team's Week 9 victory over the Washington Commanders. Nacua is also set to be a free agent this coming offseason now that his rookie deal is set to expire, and Rams head coach Sean McVay delivered a mixed message about Nacua's future with the team.

"Yeah, we have a lot of guys that are free agents," McVay told reporters earlier this week. "What I've tried to really do is focus on right here, right now. He's obviously a guy that is a very important piece for us for now and for the future, but there are a lot of guys that fall under that category."

That makes it sound like Nacua will be back with the Rams, and there's not much to speculate about. But a later quote indicated there may not be as much certainty on that front, mostly because McVay said those words pretty much exactly.

"I can't say for certain anything," McVay said. "Here's what I'm not interested in: something being taken out of context because my focus and concentration are on a Friday practice, even though I know it's Monday. I am trying to see how well we can play as a team against an excellent opponent [the Green Bay Packers] on Wednesday night.

"When you go through the amount of free agents that we have, Puka is a huge part of the conversation that you love, but there are also guys that are part of his draft class. There are guys on our offensive line, there are some guys defensively — so there are a lot of guys that are up that, as of right now, would not be under contract. There are mechanics that we'd like to be able to try to figure out how to keep these really good players and people that we love, and certainly Puka is at the forefront of our mind."

In addition to Nacua, the Rams have Kevin Dotson, Coleman Shelton, Steve Avila, Byron Young, Josh Wallace, Colby Parkinson, Davis Allen, Davante Adams, Omar Speights and Kobie Turner, among others, set to hit free agency this offseason. While the Rams' $75.2 million in projected cap space is the fifth-most in the league (according to Over the Cap), that's a lot of players. Many of the Rams' pending free agents are significant contributors. However, none of them is nearly as integral to the team's success as Nacua is.

Nacua is the Rams' best offensive player. He is one of the best receivers in the league, and he's well on his way to being one of the best in recent memory if he can stay healthy. His 383 catches are the seventh-most all time through four seasons despite the fact that he's only played 3.5 years so far. His 4,906 receiving yards are the seventh-most as well. He's the all-time leader in receiving yards per game (96.2), and he's averged over 100 yards per game in each of the last two seasons.

But he's also somewhat unreliable from a health perspective, as a regular visitor to the medical tent and someone who will have missed 17 of the team's 51 games over the last three seasons by the time this year is up. And he's had very public off-field issues over the last year or so that resulted in a three-game suspension for violating the league's personal conduct policy. The league reportedly did not know Nacua needed season-ending surgery when it suspended him and allowed him to serve the suspension during his stint on injured reserve.

It wouldn't be surprising, then, if the Rams were at least somewhat hesitant to commit what it would take to secure a long-term contract. The best wide receivers in the league are making over $40 million per year. Jaxson Smith-Njigba averages $42.5 million per year on his extension. To lock Nacua in, it would likely take a deal that exceeds JSN's average annual value, given Nacua's track record.

Meanwhile, the franchise tag is projected to be worth "only" $30.91 million next season, according to Over the Cap, so that may be an option for the Rams to explore instead. That would allow them to retain Nacua for at least next season, even if they don't reach a long-term agreement, while also letting them negotiate an extension and retain the ability to explore potential trade opportunities if they decide they don't want to commit to him long term. And it seems like him not being around long-term is at least a possibility in the ether.

"Very uncertain, up in the air as it pertains to the future with the L.A. Rams because going into free agency he's got two different injuries, including a significant MCL injury that Sean McVay says will keep him out a few months," ESPN's Jeremy Fowler said this weekend. "Probably ends his tenure with the Rams — plus the three-game suspension for the off-field stuff this offseason, so it's just not the kind of way you want to go into free agency with momentum. On the field, he's the best free agent in 2027 of any player, so the Rams have got to sort that out."

Fowler may have misspoken when he said the injury probably ends Nacua's tenure with the Rams. Based on the rest of the quote, it seems like he meant that the injury will end Nacua's season with the Rams. But the idea that his future is uncertain at all is obviously notable, given how important he is to the team. If Nacua isn't going to be on the team, then the Rams don't have much to build their offense around in the future, whenever the post-Matthew Stafford era begins. They wouldn't exactly be setting Ty Simpson up for success if they decided to go that route.

Because Nacua is so good and so important to the Rams' offensive infrastructure, it seems likely they'll eventually come to an agreement on an extension. But the lack of certainty in that regard, both from McVay and in outside reporting, makes this situation one to watch.

#2551. Ranking NFL division races from first to worst: NFC North, NFC South entertaining for very different reasons

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NFC East might be the best example of the NFL's unpredictable nature. Earlier this season, it made history by becoming the first division to go winless over a two-week span in which every team played both weeks. Yes, that included the infamous Commanders-Giants tie that featured a fumble and an all-time clock mismanagement on the final two drives.

Then in Week 11, the division went 4-0 collectively, with the Eagles, Giants, and Commanders all springing upsets over AFC teams currently in the playoff field. A $10 NFC East parlay of the Eagles beating the Steelers, the Giants beating the Jaguars, the Commanders beating the Bengals and the Cowboys beating the Titans would have netted you a handsome $345.51.

As Al Pacino, playing Michael Corleone in The Godfather Part III, said: "Just when I thought I was out, they pull me back in!"

Ahead of a packed Thanksgiving week chock full of divisional matchups, we rank all eight division races, taking into account the quality of the teams involved, the quality of the races themselves and the potential for pandemonium.

The NFC North's main quest is potentially being the first team to place all four teams in the postseason. But the division race itself is a thriller, especially with Lions-Bears looming on Thanksgiving. Yes, Detroit looks like the clear NFC North favorite for now, but a Chicago win on Turkey Day would boost the Bears' chance to win the division to 45%. Regardless, this race projects to end in a thriller: In Week 18, the Lions play the Packers, and the Bears play the Vikings.

Does it get much better than a 50/50 split? Technically, our projections give Denver a 50.1% chance and Kansas City a 49.9% chance, if you're into that level of detail. The two teams have already played both of their head-to-head matchups (they split). The Broncos do have, on paper, an easier schedule remaining, which certainly helps.

All of a sudden, this division race doesn't look fun-bad and might just be ... fun! The Giants and Cowboys have the eighth- and ninth-hardest remaining schedules, while the Commanders don't face a team with a winning record until Week 16. A finishing stretch featuring Giants at Cowboys in Week 17 followed by Cowboys at Commanders and Eagles at Giants in Week 18 could provide plenty of twists and turns.

Last year, the Buccaneers beat the Panthers in Week 18 to stay alive, only to lose the NFC South on a tiebreaker the next day when the Falcons beat the Saints. Could we see similar madness this year? Week 12 will go a long way: If Tampa Bay beats Carolina on Monday Night Football, its chance to win the division jumps to 53%, per our calculations.

The NFC South: It might be bad, but it's certainly not boring!

Even with the bunched standings at the top, our projections see Cincinnati as a clear favorite. The Bengals have several games where they should be huge favorites: Saints, at Panthers, at Colts, Ravens. It's far from wrapped up, though, and two games vs. the Browns loom large.

The 49ers look like the best team in the NFL, and with a three-game lead in the division, this one might not have much drama. If that changes, it must start this week, when the Seahawks visit San Francisco. A Seattle win would only knock the 49ers' NFC West title chances to 81%, but it'd be a start.

Never say never, but it's hard to see this one getting competitive, even after the Texans won and the Jaguars lost in Week 11. Houston needs another upset loss or two by Jacksonville. If that happens, remember Houston holds the head-to-head tiebreaker. That could turn up the heat.

With Drake Maye out until the final week or two at best, it would take something catastrophic (basically a Josh Allen injury) for this to be an actual race. And then, Tommy DeVito trying to chase down Kyle Allen would be more sad than fun.
